(iii) Core degeneracies (η_X–f_b–z, Φ–Ṁ through φ, N_H(t)–Γ(t) in-band) are acknowledged, but the proposed external constraints (optical/radio upper limits, host magnitude redshift prior) may be too weak to yield decisive Bayes factors; the discrimination claim could collapse to comparing flexible parametric families. (iv) The competing models are not matched in flexibility: a magnetar model with a simple spin-down law is far less expressive than the bespoke flux-loss transition; unless model complexity is rigorously controlled (e.g., equalized effective degrees of freedom and shared spectral/absorption systematics), out-of-sample failure could reflect capacity mismatch rather than physics. Overall, this is a well-engineered inference pipeline with a plausible MAD/BZ narrative, but the causal linkage from MAD exit to a near-achromatic NICER/XRT crash and the promised spectral signature needs tighter microphysical closure and complexity control to be logically compelling as a discriminant.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the precursor emission and the observed quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in GRB 211211A are produced by discrete, tidal-stress–driven yielding episodes in the crust of a magnetar component during the last ~10^2–10^3 s of inspiral, and that the QPO frequencies trace excitation of a specific magneto-elastic mode family (torsional crustal modes hybridized with core Alfvén continua) whose eigenfrequencies and damping are controlled by the internal magnetic field and equation of state (EoS). The proposal resolves the reviewers’ identified bottlenecks by replacing the ill-posed notion of “nonlinear Love-number modification” with a rigorously closed forward-modeling stack: (i) an explicitly stated inspiral/trajectory framework (PN/EOB orbital driver) matched to (ii) a GR perturbation calculation on a TOV background to compute the time-dependent tidal stress field inside an elastic, dissipative crust up to a physically defined yield criterion, which then seeds (iii) a reduced magneto-elastic excitation and magnetosphere-coupling model that predicts both the timing/energetics of precursor energy release and the QPO frequency evolution. This architecture produces falsifiable, phase-resolved predictions linking orbital phase → crustal failure cadence → released energy → mode frequencies, and yields discriminants against non-tidal alternatives (e.g., accretion-powered precursors or jet-instability QPOs) through the predicted chirp-like evolution and orbital-phase locking of the QPOs and failure episodes.
Plan:
1) Choose a single, internally consistent spacetime/trajectory framework and matching conditions.
   1.1 Inspiral driver: use an EOB (effective-one-body) or 3.5PN TaylorT4 orbital phase evolution including standard adiabatic tides (linear) and spin-orbit terms up to a stated order (baseline: 3.5PN point-mass + leading-order tidal phase corrections). This provides r(t), Ωorb(t), and the companion’s tidal field multipoles as functions of time.
   1.2 Stellar background: construct a non-rotating (or slow-rotation Hartle–Thorne at O(χ)) TOV magnetar model for each candidate EoS. Fix M, R, and crust thickness from the EoS; treat the internal magnetic field as a parameterized axisymmetric configuration that enters the magneto-elastic step (below) rather than the background metric.
   1.3 Matching: compute the external quadrupolar tidal field from the PN/EOB trajectory and match it to the GR even-parity l=2 metric perturbation boundary condition at the stellar surface (standard tidal perturbation matching). Deliverable: a verified r(t), Ω(t) pipeline consistent with the GR perturbation boundary conditions.

2) Compute a time-dependent tidal stress/strain field in the crust (abandon “Love-number modification”).
   2.1 Linear GR tidal response (pre-yield): solve the static/low-frequency GR perturbation equations for the l=2 tidal deformation on a TOV background to obtain the strain/stress tensor distribution in the crust as a function of instantaneous tidal field amplitude Eij(t). Use the “instantaneous equilibrium” approximation while explicitly validating it against the orbital timescale (Ωorb) and crustal shear-wave crossing time; state the regime of validity (late inspiral but before strong dynamical tide resonance).
   2.2 Elastic constitutive law: implement an isotropic Coulomb solid crust with shear modulus μ(ρ, T, Z, impurity) using standard microphysical fits; include temperature dependence through a prescribed thermal profile and include a Maxwell visco-elastic element (Kelvin–Voigt or standard linear solid) to model dissipation and stress relaxation on a timescale τvisc.
   2.3 Yield criterion and dissipation: adopt a von Mises yield criterion with breaking strain εbreak(T, impurity) (baseline range 0.01–0.1) and implement plastic flow/heating when σVM exceeds σyield. Parameterize plastic dissipation via an effective plastic viscosity ηpl and compute local heating ΔT from dissipated work, updating μ(T) self-consistently (magneto-thermal feedback at reduced order).
   2.4 Output: a time series of yielding events defined by when/where σVM crosses threshold, yielding episode duration, dissipated energy Eheat, and a “failure patch” size and location on the crust. Deliverable: orbital-phase–tagged failure catalog and energy budget.

3) Specify the magnetic coupling pathway with a concrete reduced magneto-elastic model and QPO identification.
   3.1 Mode family selection (operational QPO mapping): identify the QPOs with torsional (axial) magneto-elastic oscillations: crustal torsional shear modes coupled to core Alfvén continua in the presence of an internal B-field (Bint). This is the only mode family carried forward in the baseline model.
   3.2 Eigenmode computation (reduced model): compute torsional magneto-elastic eigenfrequencies and damping using a 1D/2D axisymmetric model: (i) elastic crust with μ(ρ,T), (ii) magnetized fluid core with Alfvén speed vA(B,ρ), and (iii) coupling at the crust-core boundary. Use established magneto-elastic wave equations in the Cowling approximation (δgμν=0) as the baseline; justify this approximation for frequency predictions (QPOs) versus GW phase modeling.
   3.3 Excitation by failure: map each failure patch to an impulse/forcing term that injects energy into the torsional displacement field (initial condition Δξφ localized to the patch, amplitude set by released elastic + magnetic stress energy). Compute resulting mode amplitudes and the expected QPO spectrum and its time evolution as Ωorb increases and the failure patch distribution changes.
   3.4 Magnetosphere and radiation channel: couple surface torsional motion to a force-free magnetosphere using a boundary driving prescription (twist angle Δψ(t) proportional to surface shear). Parameterize the conversion from injected magnetospheric energy to observable gamma-ray precursor fluence with an efficiency εrad and beaming factor fb; treat these as nuisance parameters in inference.
   3.5 Output: predicted QPO frequencies (and their drift), quality factors (damping), and precursor light-curve morphology (timing/fluence) tied to orbital phase and failure episodes.

4) Forward model: explicit mapping from orbital phase → failures → emission/QPOs, plus discriminant predictions.
   4.1 Scaling relations (deliverable-ready): derive and numerically validate scalings:
       • Failure cadence: Δt between failures decreases with increasing tidal field ∝ r(t)^{-3}; predict a monotonic acceleration of event rate approaching merger.
       • Failure timing/phase locking: events cluster near specific orbital phases if the stress pattern is dominated by l=2 geometry; predict correlation with orbital phase (modulo precession if included).
       • QPO frequency set: fQPO ≈ f_torsional(Bint,EoS,crust thickness) with weak dependence on orbital frequency, but with possible stepwise changes when heating/plasticity changes μ(T).
       • Energy per event: Eevent ≈ ∫(σ:Δε)dV over failure patch plus magnetic untwisting energy; predict a bounded distribution with a high-end cutoff controlled by εbreak and patch size.
   4.2 Discriminants vs competing scenarios:
       (D1) Orbital-phase locking: tidal model predicts precursor sub-structure/QPO onset times tied to Ωorb(t); accretion/jet-instability models generally do not predict phase-locked repetition tied to a calculable inspiral chirp.
       (D2) Frequency clustering: torsional magneto-elastic QPOs should appear in discrete bands tied to EoS/Bint, rather than broadband or drifting purely with jet dynamics.
       (D3) Precursor-to-merger timing relation: predicted window of activity begins when σVM first reaches yield at a calculable separation; this provides a falsifiable relation between precursor lead time and binary parameters.

5) Inference framework with explicit likelihood, nuisance parameters, and identifiability tests.
   5.1 Data model: use observed precursor light curve (event times, durations, fluences) and QPO measurements (frequencies, uncertainties, quality factors, time stamps). Optionally incorporate constraints on distance and host environment as priors.
   5.2 Likelihood:
       • Timing: Poisson (or clustered point-process) likelihood for failure events with rate λ(t|θ) predicted by the stress/yield model.
       • Fluence: lognormal likelihood for event fluences given Eevent with nuisance parameters εrad and fb; marginalize over (εrad, fb).
       • QPOs: Gaussian likelihood in measured fQPO(t) with model frequencies from eigenmode solver; include a mixture model for multiple mode identifications if needed.
   5.3 Priors: EoS prior from maximum mass and causality; Bint prior broad log-uniform (10^14–10^16 G internal), εbreak prior informed by crust simulations; distance/beaming priors from GRB population constraints.
   5.4 Synthetic recovery / identifiability: generate mock datasets from the forward model across a grid of (EoS, Bint, εbreak, τvisc) and perform Bayesian recovery to demonstrate which parameters are identifiable and which are degenerate with εrad/fb. Deliverable: identifiability report and required data quality thresholds.

6) Validation and robustness checks.
   6.1 Consistency checks: verify stress field against Newtonian elastic limits in weak-field regime; verify energy conservation between tidal work, dissipated heat, and injected mode energy.
   6.2 Sensitivity tests: vary thermal profile, impurity parameter, and viscosity model; quantify impact on predicted failure cadence and QPO damping.
   6.3 Extension path (optional, not baseline): incorporate dynamical tide resonances if the orbital frequency approaches relevant mode frequencies; include slow rotation and precession only after baseline closure.

Deliverables (explicit): (A) a phase-resolved failure catalog as a function of EoS/Bint; (B) a QPO frequency atlas tied to magneto-elastic mode family with damping predictions; (C) a precursor forward model generating light curves conditioned on inspiral parameters; (D) a full Bayesian inference code with synthetic recovery demonstrating identifiability; (E) at least one falsifiable discriminant (orbital-phase locking + frequency banding) benchmarked against non-tidal alternatives.
Feasibility:
1) Closed, approximation-driven modeling stack (addresses internal inconsistency).
   The proposal now commits to a single coherent architecture: PN/EOB provides the inspiral trajectory and tidal field; GR perturbations on a TOV background provide the interior tidal stress field; nonlinearity enters only through a physically defined yield/plasticity law, not through redefined Love numbers. Magnetic/radiative complexity is confined to a reduced magneto-elastic + force-free coupling model whose assumptions are stated (Cowling approximation for mode frequencies; parameterized radiative efficiency), avoiding gauge inconsistencies from mixing “fully relativistic” claims with under-defined PN dynamics.

2) Love-number issue resolved (addresses critique ii).
   Love numbers remain in their proper role (linear response descriptor) and are not modified to represent nonlinear failure. Instead, the key computed quantity is σVM(t,r,θ) in the crust and its crossing of a specified yield surface, including dissipation and heating—an executable route to failure predictions.

3) Magnetic coupling made operational (addresses critique iii).
   Crust failure is mapped to a concrete excitation mechanism for a specified QPO-producing mode family: torsional magneto-elastic oscillations (crustal torsional modes hybridized with core Alfvén continua). The proposal explicitly computes eigenfrequencies/damping and uses a boundary-driving prescription to connect surface shear to magnetospheric twist and radiative output, with εrad and beaming treated as nuisance parameters rather than assumed constants.

4) Observables operationalized with falsifiable predictions (addresses critique iv).
   The forward model provides explicit outputs: (i) event timing distributions and their orbital-phase dependence; (ii) precursor fluence distributions with a calculable high-end cutoff; (iii) QPO frequency bands and stepwise evolution tied to μ(T) changes from dissipation. Discriminants are stated: orbital-phase locking and discrete frequency banding are expected in the tidal-failure model but not generically in accretion-powered or jet-instability scenarios.

5) Inference defined and testable (addresses critique v).
   A likelihood is specified for timing, fluence, and QPO frequencies with clear nuisance parameters (distance, beaming, radiative efficiency) explicitly marginalized. Identifiability is not assumed; it is demonstrated via synthetic recovery tests to show which combinations of (EoS, Bint, εbreak, viscosity) can be constrained by the available observables.

6) Empirical and literature anchoring.
   The physical pathway is directly grounded in the established tidal-force–induced crust breaking framework for magnetars in compact binaries (Asset 2) and the broader motivation to connect compact-object interaction dynamics to periodic or quasi-periodic high-energy/radio phenomenology (Asset 1 provides contextual support that compact binaries can imprint periodic activity). The proposed deliverables are therefore not speculative extensions but controlled refinements that convert the concept chain into a quantitative, falsifiable, and computationally tractable program.
Critique: This is an unusually well-resolved proposal that directly addresses prior conceptual bottlenecks and demonstrates strong control over both relativistic inspiral physics and neutron-star microphysics. The engineering plan is detailed, executable, and avoids category errors (e.g., conflating linear tidal response with nonlinear failure). Logical consistency is high: the causal chain from orbital phase to stress accumulation, yielding, mode excitation, and observable QPOs is explicitly constructed and closed. Minor deductions arise from residual idealizations that may limit quantitative accuracy: (i) reliance on the instantaneous-equilibrium approximation deep into late inspiral without a clearly quantified breakdown threshold, (ii) Cowling-approximation magneto-elastic mode calculations that may bias damping/Q predictions, and (iii) substantial degeneracy risk between internal magnetic-field geometry and effective crustal heating in the inference stage. Evidence grounding is strong and remains anchored to compact-object tidal physics and magnetar phenomenology, though observational anchoring to the specific GRB 211211A dataset (signal-to-noise limits, QPO significance, and selection effects) could be more explicit. The rationale is creative and nontrivial, reframing an ill-posed idea into a falsifiable forward model, but still builds on a known theoretical pathway rather than introducing a fundamentally new physical mechanism.

Hypothesis: Coherent radio bursts (including nanoshots associated with pulsar Type II emission) are produced when plasmoid mergers in the magnetospheric current sheet just beyond the light cylinder trigger fast-magnetosonic wave packets whose phase coherence is preserved by a reconnection-driven, charge-starved parallel electric field (E||) that also initiates hadron-loading and subsequent secondary-particle cascades. We hypothesize that the joint occurrence and timing of (i) plasmoid-merger electromagnetic precursors and (ii) nuclear/secondary-particle signatures are controlled by a single dimensionless control parameter, \(\Pi \equiv \sigma_{LC}\,\tau_{rec}\,\Omega\) (magnetization at the LC times reconnection timescale times spin), which sets the plasmoid hierarchy and the radiative coherence bandwidth. Methodological adaptation: extend standard PIC reconnection simulations to a physically constrained, multi-species radiation-kinetic PIC framework by (a) embedding a relativistic resistive-force-free (RFF) global magnetosphere solution as a dynamically consistent boundary/driver for local PIC patches across the LC current sheet, and (b) adding a baryon/meson production + decay module implemented as a conservative Monte-Carlo collision operator that enforces exact energy-momentum and charge conservation at each event, enabling self-consistent coupling between reconnection microphysics, coherent radio emission, and Type II-like secondary particle production.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Build a global rotating magnetosphere solution (RFF / GRFFE) for a set of pulsar/magnetar-like parameters spanning \(B_{LC}\), \(\Omega\), and inclination; extract time-dependent boundary fields, currents, and plasma injection prescriptions at and beyond the light cylinder.
1.2 Select observational targets with known coherent bursts (e.g., Crab-like nanoshots; intermittent coherent bursts from radio-quiet/X-ray-bright neutron stars) and compile contemporaneous constraints (spin, \(\dot\nu\), distance, X-ray luminosity). Define prediction metrics: burst energy distribution, nanoshot duration, polarization swings, and phase alignment with high-energy emission.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Patch-based coupled simulation: deploy multiple local PIC domains tiled along the equatorial current sheet beyond the LC, each driven by the global RFF boundary conditions (fields + Poynting flux + injected pair density). Implement a two-way coupling by feeding back coarse-grained effective conductivity/particle loading from PIC to the global model on timescales \(\gtrsim\Omega^{-1}\) while preserving causality (no superluminal information transfer; explicit time-lagged updates).
2.2 Conservative radiation-kinetic extension: augment PIC with (i) curvature/synchrotron radiation reaction for leptons and (ii) a nuclear/secondary module: baryon injection tied to reconnection heating (parameterized initially by an ion fraction \(f_i\) but evolved by local charge-starvation criteria), followed by inelastic p-\(\gamma\) and p-p channels producing mesons; implement meson decay into secondary leptons/photons as a Monte-Carlo operator that exactly conserves 4-momentum and charge per interaction and respects threshold kinematics.
2.3 Coherent emission extraction without black-box assumptions: compute far-field radio emission from the simulated current density \(\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x},t)\) using retarded potentials; isolate fast-magnetosonic wave packets launched by plasmoid mergers and quantify phase coherence via cross-spectral density across the emitting region. Enforce numerical constraints: divergence cleaning for \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0\), charge conservation via current deposition schemes, and resolution studies to ensure plasmoid hierarchy convergence.
2.4 Mechanism tests: deliberately control \(\Pi\) by varying \(\sigma_{LC}\), reconnection rate (via guide field and effective resistivity), and \(\Omega\); quantify how the plasmoid merger rate, secondary-sheet formation, and wave-packet coherence scale with \(\Pi\). Run counterfactual suites: lepton-only vs lepton+ion; suppressed E|| vs self-consistent E||; to isolate the causal role of charge starvation and hadron-loading.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Validation against known Type II emission phenomenology: compare simulated nanoshot duration distributions and GHz-band brightness temperatures to Crab-like constraints; test predicted phase relation between radio nanoshots and high-energy pulses (from simulated curvature/synchrotron emissivity maps folded by rotation).
3.2 Multi-messenger/nuclear physics linkage: compute predicted neutrino spectra and secondary gamma-ray components from meson decay; derive joint constraints on ion fraction \(f_i\) and magnetospheric potential drops consistent with nuclear thresholds. Use these to place bounds on magnetospheric baryon loading that feed back to neutron-star surface composition/EOS inferences (via allowed outflow mass loading and pair multiplicity requirements).
3.3 Uncertainty quantification: perform Bayesian calibration over \(f_i\), injection multiplicity, and reconnection parameters using physically constrained priors (causality, energy budget from spin-down, and charge/current closure). Report posterior predictive distributions for burst rates and energetics, and identify falsifiable signatures: (i) a tight scaling of coherence bandwidth with \(\Pi\); (ii) correlated enhancement of secondary signatures when E||-driven charge starvation is strongest; (iii) polarization angle swings tied to secondary current-sheet formation during plasmoid mergers.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 2 provides first-principles evidence that plasmoid mergers in the current sheet beyond the light cylinder generate coherent radio emission (nanoshots) via fast-magnetosonic waves; Asset 1 establishes that coherent bursts can arise even from historically radio-quiet neutron stars, motivating a mechanism that can switch on intermittently. Reconnection, plasmoid instability, and retarded-potential radiation extraction are mature techniques; radiation-reaction PIC is established; conservative Monte-Carlo collision operators with exact 4-momentum conservation are standard in high-energy transport.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The key limitation of existing PIC studies is incomplete closure between global magnetospheric electrodynamics and local kinetic reconnection, and the omission of nuclear/secondary channels that can become relevant when charge starvation produces large E|| and hadron loading. The proposed RFF-to-PIC patch coupling preserves Maxwell constraints and causal information flow while allowing microphysics to modify effective conductivity and particle loading. The nuclear module is implemented as a conservation-law-preserving operator consistent with threshold kinematics, maintaining strict adherence to physical laws.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with stand-alone local PIC or purely global force-free models, the adapted multi-scale, multi-species framework can (i) predict absolute burst energetics from the spin-down-fed Poynting flux, (ii) generate directly comparable observables (radio waveforms, spectra, polarization) from first principles, and (iii) produce falsifiable multi-messenger correlations (secondary gamma/neutrino components) that constrain magnetospheric baryon loading and, indirectly, neutron-star surface composition/EOS. This turns coherent radio bursts from phenomenological signatures into quantitative probes of magnetospheric current closure and high-energy/nuclear processes near the light cylinder.
Critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-constructed proposal that targets a genuine bottleneck in pulsar/magnetar radio-burst theory: the lack of closure between global electrodynamics, kinetic reconnection, and observable coherent emission. The engineering plan is unusually explicit, particularly regarding causal two-way coupling, charge conservation, retarded-potential emission extraction, and controlled counterfactual suites. The introduction of a dimensionless control parameter \(\Pi = \sigma_{LC}\tau_{rec}\Omega\) is conceptually attractive and testable, though its uniqueness and scaling justification are asserted rather than derived. The largest weakness lies in the nuclear/secondary-particle component: while technically feasible in isolation, its necessity and expected rate in light-cylinder conditions are not quantitatively justified, and the link between hadron-loading, Type II-like radio coherence, and detectable multi-messenger signatures risks being overextended. The proposal occasionally conflates plausibility with inevitability (e.g., charge starvation generically leading to significant hadron loading). Nonetheless, the logical chain from plasmoid mergers to coherent fast-magnetosonic emission is internally consistent and grounded in contemporary reconnection literature.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that equation-of-state (EoS)–dependent angular-momentum redistribution in binary neutron star (BNS) remnants imprints a *coupled, measurable* signature on (i) the post-merger gravitational-wave (GW) spectral morphology and (ii) the composition–enthalpy evolution of the remnant disk and winds through neutrino-regulated electron fraction (Ye) and nuclear statistical equilibrium (NSE) freeze-out, thereby controlling r-process heating and kilonova observables. Mechanistically: (1) EoS stiffness sets the remnant’s compactness and differential-rotation profile, which fixes the efficiency and timescale of magnetic braking/MRI-driven angular momentum transport from the core to the disk. (2) That angular-momentum flux controls the disk’s mass reservoir, accretion rate onto the remnant (or BH if collapse occurs), and the strength/geometry of neutrino irradiation from the hot remnant+inner disk. (3) Neutrino irradiation and weak interactions set Ye and entropy in the outflowing material; together with the expansion timescale, they determine whether matter remains in NSE, undergoes alpha recombination, or freezes out into heavy-element nucleosynthesis (r-process), which sets the radioactive heating rate and hence the kilonova luminosity, color evolution, and late-time decline. The proposal overcomes the reviewer-identified mismatch with H/He Type-I burst phenomenology by replacing ‘surface thermonuclear burning’ with *compositionally appropriate post-merger nuclear heating/cooling channels* (NSE ↔ freeze-out, alpha recombination, r-process heating) that are unavoidable in BNS disks and are directly tied to observable kilonova spectra/light curves. The core chain remains intact—rotation profile → GW post-merger features → angular-momentum transport → disk accretion/outflows—while the second observational branch is revised to a physically consistent post-merger nucleosynthesis/opacity/heating diagnostic that is EoS-sensitive through the same angular-momentum and neutrino-irradiation pathways.
Plan:
Step 1 — Controlled GR initial data and EoS suite (rotation-profile control):
1.1 Generate constraint-satisfying BNS initial data (same total gravitational mass, mass ratio, and initial orbital angular momentum) for ≥3 finite-temperature, composition-dependent tabulated EoSs spanning soft/intermediate/stiff.
1.2 Include consistent temperature and composition variables required by each EoS table (ρ, T, Ye) and ensure causal sound speed and thermodynamic consistency checks (Maxwell relations where applicable).

Step 2 — GRMHD with stated microphysics set (what is added, explicitly):
2.1 Evolve in full GRMHD including magnetic-field amplification (winding + MRI). Use a divergence-cleaning or constrained-transport scheme; specify target quality factors for MRI: Qθ, Qφ ≥ 10 in the disk (or document where unmet).
2.2 Neutrino treatment: implement a grey (energy-integrated) leakage scheme as baseline for cooling *plus* an M1 moment scheme (or approximate two-moment closure) for irradiation in follow-up runs to quantify systematics. Track νe, ν̅e absorption/emission rates.
2.3 Ye evolution: evolve a conservative Ye advection equation with source terms from charged-current weak interactions consistent with the neutrino scheme; enforce Ye ∈ [0,1] and couple to the EoS table.
2.4 Nuclear thermodynamics: include an NSE module valid at high T (e.g., T ≳ 5–6 GK) providing composition, binding energy, and pressure contributions consistent with the EoS; implement a switch/bridge to non-NSE as T drops, carrying nuclear binding energy consistently.
2.5 Non-NSE network for heating: in outflows (identified by Bernoulli/escape criteria) integrate a reduced r-process–capable heating prescription (calibrated to representative full networks) that returns time-dependent radioactive heating ẋ(t, Ye, s, τexp). Include alpha recombination energy release when transitioning from free nucleons to α-particles at relevant T/ρ.
2.6 Photodisintegration: include endothermic dissociation at high temperatures (inner disk shocks) by coupling to NSE/binding-energy bookkeeping, preventing spurious net heating.

Step 3 — Diagnostics: define the mapping rotation → GW → angular momentum flux → disk state (explicit, reviewer-requested):
3.1 Extract GW strain and compute post-merger spectral features: dominant f2 peak (and secondary peaks where resolved), time-dependent instantaneous frequency, and damping time proxies.
3.2 Compute remnant rotation profile Ω(r,θ) and differential-rotation measure (e.g., ΔΩ between core and outer layers). Quantify angular momentum transport via Maxwell + Reynolds stresses and compute the angular-momentum flux into the disk J̇disk(t).
3.3 Measure accretion rate Ṁ(t) through a control surface around the remnant (or BH horizon if collapse) and relate Ṁ(t) to neutrino luminosities Lν(t) and mean energies (if available in M1).
3.4 Track disk/outflow state variables: Ye, entropy s, expansion time τexp, and when/where NSE breaks. Record mass histograms in (Ye, s, τexp) for each EoS.

Step 4 — Predict observables tied to kilonovae (replace Type-I bursts with measurable targets):
4.1 From outflow properties, compute lanthanide/actinide fraction proxies using Ye thresholds (e.g., Ye ≲ 0.25 lanthanide-rich) and estimate opacity regimes (high-κ vs low-κ components).
4.2 Use the simulated radioactive heating rate and ejecta parameters (Mej, vej, composition classes) to generate kilonova light-curve/spectral predictions via radiative-transfer post-processing (or calibrated semi-analytic models as a first pass).
4.3 Quantify EoS-dependent differences in: total ejecta mass, velocity distribution, blue/red component ratio, and heating rate normalization/temporal slope.

Step 5 — Validation targets that are actually measurable (per directive):
5.1 GW: do not claim current LIGO/Virgo post-merger peak detections; instead, produce predictions for 3G detectors (Einstein Telescope/Cosmic Explorer) and develop ‘proxy’ correlations between inspiral-measured parameters (tidal deformability) and post-merger spectral morphology within this framework.
5.2 EM: compare predicted disk masses and ejecta properties to multi-messenger constraints from observed kilonovae (e.g., ejecta mass/velocity/color evolution classes), and to short-GRB afterglow energy budget consistency where relevant.
5.3 Remnant lifetime: infer EoS-dependent collapse time distributions and map to expected neutrino irradiation duration and resulting Ye shifts; compare with observationally inferred presence/absence of a long-lived remnant in events with well-characterized kilonova components.

Step 6 — Numerical credibility and convergence (explicit criteria):
6.1 Perform resolution studies demonstrating stability of: GW spectral peaks (within stated tolerance), disk mass, ejecta mass, and Ye distributions. Report MRI quality factors and document regions where subgrid modeling may be required.
6.2 Systematics sweep: bracket uncertainties by (i) leakage vs M1 neutrinos, (ii) alternative viscosity/subgrid prescriptions if MRI under-resolved, and (iii) alternate reduced-heating calibrations. Propagate these to kilonova predictions to show robustness of EoS trends.
Feasibility:
1) Physical appropriateness (addresses the key critique): Post-merger disks are neutron-rich and hot; the dominant, inevitable thermonuclear/nuclear channels are NSE ↔ freeze-out, alpha recombination, and r-process radioactive heating in outflows under neutrino-regulated Ye evolution—not H/He Type-I bursting. The revised proposal targets these channels and links them to kilonova observables (luminosity, color, spectra), which are the established EM counterparts to BNS mergers.

2) Microphysics completeness (avoids ‘numerical artifact’ risk): The proposal explicitly includes neutrino cooling/irradiation (leakage baseline + M1 follow-up), conservative Ye evolution with weak-interaction source terms, temperature/composition-dependent tabulated EoS coupling, binding-energy-consistent NSE treatment including photodisintegration and alpha recombination, and a domain-appropriate r-process heating prescription for outflows. These are the controlling terms for thermal balance and composition in the immediate post-merger environment.

3) Coherent mechanistic chain (preserves original concept): The EoS controls remnant compactness and differential rotation → sets angular momentum transport efficiency (MRI/winding stresses) → sets disk mass and accretion history → sets neutrino irradiation and Ye evolution → sets nucleosynthesis/heating/opacity → sets kilonova observables. In parallel, the same rotation profile governs the post-merger GW spectral morphology. This yields a coupled GW+EM discriminator of the EoS that does not rely on inappropriate LMXB burst phenomenology.

4) Observational credibility (revised validation): The plan aligns with what is currently measurable (kilonova ejecta properties) and what is plausibly measurable with near-future detectors (3G post-merger GW features), avoiding claims about current LIGO/Virgo post-merger spectroscopy.

5) Computational feasibility: GRMHD merger simulations with leakage neutrinos and Ye evolution are established; adding an NSE module plus reduced r-process heating for outflows is a tractable extension. The plan includes explicit convergence/MRI-quality diagnostics and a systematics program (leakage vs M1; resolution) to ensure inferred EoS trends are not artifacts.
Critique: The proposal is methodologically ambitious and largely well-specified, with an unusually clear causal chain from EoS-dependent rotation profiles to stresses/J̇ into the disk, to Ṁ and neutrino irradiation, to Ye/entropy/freeze-out and kilonova heating/opacity—while simultaneously predicting post-merger GW spectral morphology for 3G detectors. The main weaknesses are (i) quantification risk: the central claim of a *coupled, measurable* GW–EM signature is not backed by an explicit statistical identifiability plan (e.g., how degeneracies with total mass, mass ratio, initial B-field topology, neutrino-transport systematics, and viewing angle will be separated from EoS effects), and (ii) numerical risk: resolving MRI (Q≳10) in global BNS remnants/disks at feasible cost is often not achieved; without a concrete fallback (calibrated effective viscosity informed by shearing-box or high-res local studies) the angular-momentum-redistribution pillar may become resolution-dependent. A secondary consistency issue is that the proposal’s correction away from Type-I bursts is scientifically appropriate, but the target concept chain still explicitly includes 'thermonuclear burning'; the current narrative should either explicitly redefine that node as neutron-rich nuclear recombination/heating or justify the terminology in-discipline. Overall, the plan is strong but would benefit from sharper falsifiable metrics and a clearer strategy for uncertainty propagation to the claimed EoS-discriminating observables.

Hypothesis: Neutron-star binaries dynamically assembled and retained in globular clusters (GCs)—with enhanced retention supplied by low-kick accretion-induced collapse (AIC) progenitors—form a multi-messenger subpopulation whose early-time X-ray emission is frequently dominated by a mildly relativistic cocoon/wind component whose observed time–energy morphology is strongly modulated by special-relativistic Doppler boosting. The central claim is not that the neutron-star equation of state (EoS) deterministically fixes the outflow, but that the EoS induces *statistical* shifts in (i) the remnant fate (prompt collapse vs hypermassive vs supramassive NS), (ii) the disk/wind mass and velocity distribution, and (iii) the baryon-pollution/enthalpy budget that controls the attainable Lorentz-factor angular structure Γ(θ). These EoS-dependent shifts imprint a recognizable Doppler signature—joint spectral blue-shift and time compression (E→δE′, t→t′/δ) plus the beaming-induced hardness–intensity covariance—that is separable from intrinsic spectral evolution when modeled through instrument responses and absorption. We overcome the reviewers’ identifiability and overconfidence concerns by (a) replacing near-deterministic remnant→disk/B→Γ links with an uncertainty-marginalized, discrepancy-aware remnant/outflow emulator calibrated to NR/GRMHD simulation suites; (b) explicitly propagating emulator uncertainty and model discrepancy as hierarchical nuisance structure so EoS posteriors remain conservative under misspecification; (c) proving (via mutual information/Fisher and injection campaigns including upper limits) that Doppler-induced time–energy signatures remain identifiable against plausible alternatives (afterglow, fallback/accretion, magnetar nebula) across realistic observing conditions; and (d) aligning the amortized inference training distribution to the *observed* selection-biased distribution through a full yield forecast (LVK horizon × GC spatial distribution × follow-up completeness). This turns Doppler boosting from a nuisance into a partially identifiable latent variable that *probabilistically* couples to EoS through remnant/outflow statistics rather than through brittle deterministic prescriptions, enabling robust EoS constraints specifically for a GC-enhanced subpopulation.
Plan:
Step 1 — GC-anchored population prior + yield forecast (selection-aware)
1.1 Build a GC catalog and spatial prior:
  - Construct a GC database for the Milky Way + nearby galaxies out to D_max=200 Mpc (not limited to ≤5 Mpc), including: sky position, distance, GC specific frequency S_N (host-dependent), GC system mass, and (where available) proxies for escape speed and central density.
  - For the Milky Way, ingest per-cluster escape velocities, core densities, metallicities, and pulsar/X-ray-binary inventories (Chandra/XMM), as in Asset 1, but use them to constrain hyperparameters rather than define hard event selection.

1.2 AIC-retention hypermodel (Asset 1 → NS retention prior):
  - Define hyperparameters Θ_AIC={f_AIC, σ_k,AIC, σ_k,CC, μ_NS,ret(M_gc), α_dyn} where σ_k,AIC is the natal-kick dispersion for AIC, σ_k,CC for core-collapse NSs, and μ_NS,ret is a retention scaling with GC potential depth.
  - Likelihood: use observed GC pulsar counts (and completeness-corrected millisecond pulsar and LMXB counts) with a hierarchical Poisson–lognormal model; map Θ_AIC to expected retained NS counts using an escape-speed-dependent retention integral over the kick distribution.
  - Output: a GC-conditioned prior on the number of retained NSs and a dynamical-assembly prior for BNS properties (mass ratio q, component masses, possible eccentricity at formation), with uncertainty.

1.3 Multi-messenger yield forecast (mandatory):
  - Define an *observed-event rate* for GC-origin BNS mergers:
    R_obs,GC = ∫ dV(z) [R_BNS(z) × π_GC(z|S_N) × p_det,GW(θ_GW) × p_follow,X(t_start, F_lim) × p_detect,X(model, θ_X)]
  - Implement p_det,GW using LVK detection efficiency surfaces (chirp mass–distance–inclination) from injection campaigns; implement p_follow,X via a cadence model (time-to-first-XRT/NICER pointing distribution, exposure distribution, sky-visibility constraints); implement p_detect,X by forward-folding model light curves through instrument response and absorption and applying detection thresholds.
  - Deliverables:
    (i) expected number of GC-origin events per LVK run (O4/O5) with credible intervals; 
    (ii) fraction of informative X-ray non-detections (upper limits) as a function of follow-up latency;
    (iii) sensitivity of EoS information gain to follow-up strategy (optimize cadence/exposure).
  - Crucially: use this forecast to define the *training distribution* for amortized inference (Step 4), ensuring it matches the expected observed distribution, not the astrophysical intrinsic one.

Step 2 — Data layers and GW handling (avoid lossy compression)
2.1 GW likelihood interface (mandatory rigor):
  - Primary path (preferred): ingest strain-level likelihoods through public LVK infrastructure where feasible (e.g., relative binning / reduced-order quadrature likelihood evaluations) to avoid summary-statistic loss, especially for (Λ1,Λ2)–inclination–distance correlations.
  - Secondary path (if strain-level access is infeasible for some events): use a validated *sufficient-statistic compression* via conditional density estimation:
    • Train a conditional normalizing flow q(θ_GW | d_strain) on LVK injection sets to emulate the full posterior over θ_GW={m1,m2,χ1,χ2,DL,ι,Λ1,Λ2}.
    • Validate by comparing Bayes factors and posterior moments against strain-level analyses for a held-out set.
  - Selection effects: incorporate p_det,GW(θ_GW) explicitly in the hierarchical likelihood and propagate its uncertainty.

2.2 X-ray dataset assembly (Assets 2–4 relevant):
  - Curate time-tagged event data (Swift/XRT, NICER, NuSTAR, Chandra) for confirmed counterparts and for targeted follow-ups yielding upper limits.
  - Standardize: absorption model N_H with host+MW components; consistent response matrices; background treatment; log-time binning with Poisson likelihood on counts (not fluxes).
  - Construct feature representation y_X that preserves time–energy morphology: binned count spectra over multiple epochs + hardness ratios + detection/upper-limit indicators.

Step 3 — Replace deterministic remnant/outflow mapping with a calibrated emulator + discrepancy
3.1 Remnant/outflow emulator (mandatory replacement of near-deterministic links):
  - Target outputs: latent physical quantities controlling early X-rays:
    ζ = {M_disk, M_wind(θ), v_wind(θ), Y_e(θ), baryon-loading proxy B(θ), Γ(θ) distribution parameters, engine lifetime τ_eng, radiative efficiency ε_X}
  - Inputs: θ_phys={EoS parameters, m1,m2, spins, mass ratio, remnant fate class, magnetic-field prior hyperparameters}.
  - Emulator type: multi-output heteroscedastic Bayesian neural network (BNN) or deep Gaussian process (DGP) with monotonic/positivity constraints where needed (e.g., M_disk≥0) and calibrated predictive uncertainties.
  - Training data: curated NR/GRMHD simulation suites spanning EoS variety and binary parameters; include multiple codes where possible to estimate code/systematic scatter.

3.2 Explicit model discrepancy layer:
  - Introduce δ_model as an additive/multiplicative stochastic process on emulator outputs, e.g. log M_disk = log M_disk,emu + δ_disk, with δ_disk ~ Normal(0, σ_disk^2) and σ_disk given a weakly informative hyperprior informed by inter-code scatter.
  - For Γ(θ): avoid deterministic B→Γ. Parameterize Γ(θ) with a flexible angular profile (e.g., core+sheath: Γ(θ)=1+(Γ_c−1)exp(−(θ/θ_c)^2) + (Γ_s−1)exp(−(θ/θ_s)^2)) and learn (Γ_c, θ_c, Γ_s, θ_s) from emulator outputs with uncertainty; allow δ_Γ to capture unresolved physics.
  - Propagate δ_model through the inference so EoS constraints broaden appropriately under outflow uncertainty.

Step 4 — Forward emission family: expressive, multi-model, selection-aligned
4.1 Competing early-time X-ray models (prevent misspecification → EoS bias):
  - Model A (cocoon/wind; Doppler-dominated): comoving spectral template (cutoff power law or synchrotron) with evolving normalization and cutoff; Doppler mapping analytic.
  - Model B (external-shock afterglow): standard synchrotron afterglow with energy E_k, circumburst density n, microphysics (ε_e, ε_B, p), structured jet parameters; includes off-axis geometry.
  - Model C (fallback/accretion X-rays; Asset 2): fallback rate ∝ t^{-5/3} with r-process heating modulation; luminosity capped near Eddington/super-Eddington with efficiency parameter; predicts plateau-to-decay behaviors.
  - Model D (magnetar spin-down nebula): spin period P0, B_dip, ejecta optical depth evolution controlling X-ray leakage; predicts delayed brightening in some regimes.
  - Implement as a mixture-of-models with per-event discrete label k and population mixing fractions allowed to depend on GC vs field channel.

4.2 Physics-embedded Doppler layer (retain, but now within mixture model):
  - For Model A, implement exact invertible SR transforms:
    E = δ E′, t = t′/δ, F_E(t)=δ^3 F′_{E′}(t′), δ=[Γ(1−β cosθ_local)]^{-1}.
  - Couple θ_local to viewing angle and outflow angular structure.
  - Forward-fold through instrument response and absorption to predicted counts.

Step 5 — Identifiability proof-of-principle (mandatory)
5.1 Mutual information / Fisher separability study:
  - Define parameter blocks: φ_Doppler={viewing angle ι, Γ-profile params}, φ_intrinsic={intrinsic spectral-evolution params, fallback/afterglow params}, and θ_EoS.
  - Compute (via simulation) the mutual information I(φ_Doppler; y_X | instrument, N_H) and the conditional MI I(φ_Doppler; y_X | φ_intrinsic) across instruments and realistic follow-up cadences.
  - Complement with Fisher-information calculations on simplified count models to show that the joint presence of (i) spectral shift and (ii) time dilation creates an identifiable direction in parameter space distinct from intrinsic cooling/fallback scalings.

5.2 Injection campaign with upper limits included:
  - Generate injections spanning: N_H distributions, response matrices, follow-up start times (0.1–10^5 s), exposures, distances.
  - Include scenarios where only upper limits exist in early epochs; quantify how upper limits constrain δ via exclusion of boosted high-flux solutions.
  - Metrics: posterior contraction on δ and Γ-params; bias on R_1.4 and Λ_1.4 under controlled misspecification; coverage tests stratified by model label k.

Step 6 — Inference architecture: CIMF upgraded with emulator/discrepancy and correct GW usage
6.1 Constrained Invertible Multi-messenger Flow (CIMF v2):
  - Latent variables z include: EoS c_s^2(ε) knot parameters; GW source parameters; remnant fate; emulator-driven outflow parameters ζ with discrepancy δ_model; X-ray model label k; GC-origin indicator g.
  - Structure: z → (emulator + discrepancy) → outflow parameters → (Doppler layer if k=A) → instrument-folded counts.
  - Training objective: amortized posterior p(z|d_GW, d_X) with explicit selection correction using the yield-forecasted observed distribution; include categorical k via Gumbel-softmax during training for differentiability.

6.2 EoS manifold with exact physical constraints (retain, but now uncertainty-aware):
  - Parameterize c_s^2(ε) with bounded transforms enforcing 0≤c_s^2≤c^2 and monotonic thermodynamic stability; impose maximum-mass constraint with a soft prior that reflects observational uncertainty.
  - Propagate EoS uncertainty through remnant thresholds used by the emulator; avoid hard remnant-class boundaries by using probabilistic remnant-fate outputs (e.g., P_prompt, P_HMNS, P_SMNS) inferred from emulator/NR fits.

6.3 Hierarchical population model linking GC channel and EM model mix:
  - π_GC depends on host GC specific frequency and Θ_AIC; allow GC channel to shift the prior on spins/eccentricities and on model label fractions P(k|g).
  - Joint likelihood includes GW detection selection and X-ray follow-up selection (cadence-dependent censoring).

Step 7 — Validation, robustness, and deliverables
7.1 Simulation-based calibration (SBC) for EoS and Doppler parameters under each emission model and under model mismatch; require near-uniform rank statistics.
7.2 Posterior predictive checks in time–energy space (counts domain) and cross-instrument consistency.
7.3 Sensitivity analysis: quantify EoS posterior widening when (i) discrepancy variances inflated, (ii) model mix broadened, (iii) GC-rate prior weakened.
7.4 Deliverables: public code for (a) yield forecast, (b) emulator interface with uncertainty, (c) CIMF v2 inference; release trained weights and documentation for correct selection handling.
Feasibility:
Physics/astrophysics feasibility (addresses systematics): The revised design removes the proposal’s main over-identifiability risk by treating remnant→disk/wind→baryon-loading→Γ(θ) as an uncertainty-marginalized mapping calibrated to NR/GRMHD suites, with an explicit discrepancy layer capturing inter-code and unresolved-physics scatter. This ensures conservative EoS posteriors when the outflow physics is imperfectly known—directly addressing the dominant EM-side systematic identified by reviewers. The Doppler layer remains analytic and exact (SR), but Γ(θ) is no longer near-deterministic; it is inferred with calibrated uncertainty.

Model adequacy feasibility (addresses non-uniqueness of X-ray origin): Early-time X-rays in BNS mergers plausibly arise from multiple channels (cocoon/wind, afterglow, fallback/accretion, magnetar nebula). Instead of relying on a single comoving template plus a lightweight classifier, the proposal now uses an explicit mixture-of-models forward family with physically interpretable parameters and per-event model marginalization. This prevents structural misspecification from being absorbed into EoS parameters and allows conservative inference when the data do not discriminate.

Identifiability feasibility (addresses Doppler vs intrinsic evolution): The proposal now includes a mandatory, quantitative proof-of-principle: mutual-information/Fisher studies and large injection campaigns with realistic absorption, response folding, cadence, and upper limits. The separability claim is tested in the *counts domain* (not idealized flux space), ensuring it reflects actual instrument constraints. Upper limits are treated as informative censoring that can exclude strongly boosted solutions at early times.

Yield feasibility (addresses rate limitation): Rather than assuming a nearby (≤5 Mpc) GC-anchored sample, the plan provides a selection-aware yield forecast combining LVK sensitivity, GC spatial distribution (including host GC specific frequency), and realistic X-ray follow-up completeness. This forecast determines (i) whether the GC-origin subpopulation can be constrained in O4/O5 and (ii) the correct observed-distribution training set for amortized inference. The proposal also explicitly leverages non-detections and heterogeneous follow-up as constraining data, increasing effective sample size.

GW-feeds feasibility (addresses posterior recycling/summary loss): The proposal upgrades GW ingestion to either strain-level likelihood evaluation (preferred) or a validated conditional density-estimation surrogate trained and tested against strain-level analyses, explicitly preserving the tidal–inclination–distance degeneracy structure. Selection effects are incorporated in the hierarchical model rather than approximated by ad hoc efficiencies. This prevents the flow from learning artifacts due to lossy GW summaries.

Overall, the revised program remains ambitious but is now defensible: the EoS constraints arise from (a) rigorously preserved GW information, (b) Doppler-identifiable time–energy signatures tested under instrument realism, and (c) conservative marginalization over outflow-emulator uncertainty and emission-model ambiguity, with a selection-matched yield forecast ensuring the amortized training regime corresponds to what will actually be observed.
Critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-engineered: it directly addresses prior identifiability and overconfidence failure modes through (a) a calibrated emulator with discrepancy, (b) mixture-model marginalization over competing X-ray mechanisms, (c) counts-domain response folding, and (d) explicit selection modeling for both GW detection and EM follow-up. However, two core scientific risks remain insufficiently resolved. First, the central separability claim—Doppler-induced joint blue-shift/time-compression producing a hardness–intensity covariance distinguishable from intrinsic evolution—may be substantially weakened by realistic spectral-shape flexibility, evolving absorption/partial covering, and cross-calibration systematics between XRT/NICER/NuSTAR; the plan mentions N_H handling but does not specify robustness tests against time-variable absorption or calibration drift, both of which can mimic hardness evolution. Second, the EoS leverage through early X-rays is still indirectly mediated (EoS → remnant fate/disk/wind statistics → Γ(θ) distribution → Doppler signature). Even with discrepancy terms, it is not demonstrated that the remaining conditional dependence of X-ray observables on EoS is strong enough to survive marginalization over (i) model label k, (ii) Γ(θ) flexibility, (iii) radiative efficiency ε_X, and (iv) ambient density/microphysics in afterglows. The mutual-information/Fisher and injection campaigns are the right remedy, but the proposal does not pre-commit to quantitative go/no-go thresholds (e.g., minimum expected information gain on Λ1.4 or R1.4 per event and required event counts under the yield forecast). Finally, the GC-enhanced subpopulation premise hinges on several uncertain steps (GC catalog completeness to 200 Mpc; host S_N inference; mapping pulsar/LMXB counts to retained NS numbers; translating retention to BNS merger yield). These are framed hierarchically, but the compound uncertainty may dilute the claimed “GC-specific” advantage unless the forecast shows a demonstrably higher informative-event fraction than the field channel under the same follow-up constraints.

Hypothesis:
FRB 20201124A’s (a) time-variable RM—including a periodic geometric component—and (b) apparent broken power-law burst-energy statistics can be jointly and *identifiably* explained by a single magneto-ionic environment if, and only if, we adopt a concrete forward model in which a 3D MHD turbulent screen simultaneously determines Faraday rotation *and* multipath propagation observables, while the intrinsic burst-energy distribution is governed by starquake-like statistics but is mapped to detected energies through a rigorously separated (nested) intrinsic–extrinsic selection operator.

Mechanistic core (what is new and why it fixes identifiability):
1) **Single-field forward model**: We posit a statistically homogeneous, anisotropic 3D magneto-ionic turbulence field with specified joint spectra of electron-density and magnetic-field fluctuations. From this *same field*, we derive both (i) RM(t) along the line-of-sight (LoS) and (ii) scattering/ depolarization metrics (τ_sc(ν), scintillation bandwidth, and bandwidth depolarization) via the *phase* and *Faraday-depth* structure functions. This directly answers the critique that RM is a LoS integral and cannot, without additional assumptions, predict transverse scattering: we make the assumptions explicit (cross-spectra, anisotropy, inner/outer scales), include additional propagation observables in the likelihood, and demonstrate via synthetic recovery when RM-only is insufficient.
2) **Nested E–RM operator with separable intrinsic vs screen effects**: We pre-register a minimal E–RM operator with two nested hypotheses: H0 (no intrinsic dependence of polarization coherence on energy; only screen-driven completeness) vs H1 (intrinsic energy modulates an internal depolarization parameter). We require multi-band held-out prediction to select H1. This prevents the operator from absorbing arbitrary selection effects and producing a spurious energy break.
3) **Formal identifiability and cadence aliasing study**: We explicitly test whether the proposed ‘cascade-consistency’ separation between geometry and turbulence is identifiable under the real cadence/gaps by simulation-based calibration (SBC), including adversarial cases where intermittent turbulence mimics quasi-periodicity.
4) **Demoted nuclear-physics claim**: We refrain from inferring EoS weights from radiated FRB energy. Instead, we produce conservative constraints on the *available elastic energy* (upper limits / consistency checks) under explicitly parameterized radiative efficiency and beaming priors; without independent anchors, we report posterior ranges conditional on those priors, not EoS model selection.

In this refined framework, the broken power law in observed burst energies is allowed to be partially intrinsic (starquake-like) but is *falsifiably* predicted to shift in apparent break scale with observing band/time-resolution if extrinsic turbulence-driven coherence loss dominates; the periodic RM component is predicted to be phase-coherent yet *non-cascade-consistent*, enabling separation from the intermittent turbulent component using diagnostics validated under realistic sampling.
Plan:
A. Data construction (unchanged in spirit, tightened in specification)
A1. Unified burst-level catalog for FRB 20201124A across all available telescopes/bands:
- Inputs per burst: TOA, dynamic spectrum I(ν,t), Stokes Q/U/V(ν,t), fluence and S/N, time/frequency resolution, detection threshold model, calibration metadata.
- Include non-detections via survey sensitivity curves to avoid survivorship bias.
A2. RM remeasurement with a forward Q/U measurement model:
- Likelihood: (Q+iU)(ν) = (Q0+iU0) exp[2i(χ0 + RM·λ^2)] convolved with channel response; additive Gaussian noise per channel; allow for nπ ambiguity.
- Output: full posterior p(RM | data) + reliability score r_RM = 1 − P(multimodal or nπ ambiguous).
A3. Propagation observables per burst:
- Scattering: fit τ_sc(ν) from pulse broadening (where resolvable) using one-sided exponential tail or more general thin-screen kernel; otherwise upper limits.
- Scintillation: estimate Δν_d when spectral resolution permits.
- Depolarization metrics: (i) bandwidth depolarization across sub-bands, (ii) polarization angle coherence C_χ(Δν), (iii) frequency-dependent linear polarization fraction L/I(ν).

B. Mandatory Directive (1): Concrete joint forward model from a single 3D turbulence field
B1. Screen geometry and kinematics:
- Thin or thick screen parameterization with depth L and distance fraction s (source–screen–observer).
- Effective transverse velocity v_eff(t) = |(1−s) v_src(t) + s v_obs − v_scr| with priors: binary-orbital contribution for v_src(t) if geometry is present; bounded by plausible screen motions.
- Convert time lag Δt to transverse separation r = v_eff Δt.
B2. 3D anisotropic MHD turbulence specification (explicit spectral model):
- Fluctuations: δn_e(x), δB_∥(x), δB_⊥(x). Mean field B0 sets anisotropy axis.
- Power spectra (in 3D k-space):
  • P_ne(k_⊥,k_∥) = C_n^2 (k_⊥^2 + a^2 k_∥^2)^{−β/2} exp[−(k/k_i)^2] for k_o < k < ∞
  • P_B∥(k_⊥,k_∥) = C_B^2 (k_⊥^2 + a^2 k_∥^2)^{−β_B/2} exp[−(k/k_i)^2]
  • Cross-spectrum: P_{nB∥}(k) = ρ_{nB} [P_ne P_B∥]^{1/2}, with |ρ_{nB}|≤1.
- Parameters to infer (minimal set): (C_n^2, C_B^2, ρ_{nB}, β, a, l_o=2π/k_o, l_i=2π/k_i, L, s). Priors enforce physical ranges; β near 11/3 but not fixed.
B3. Derived observables from the same field (explicit links):
- RM along LoS: RM(t) = K ∫_0^L [n_0 + δn_e(x)] [B0,∥ + δB_∥(x)] dz + RM_geo(φ_orb(t))
  where K is the Faraday constant; RM_geo is the periodic geometric component (see Section C).
- Faraday-depth fluctuations and depolarization:
  • Faraday depth φ(θ) = K ∫ n_e B_∥ dz as a function of sky angle θ across the scattered image.
  • Bandwidth depolarization predicted from Var(φ) across the effective beam/image: p(λ) ≈ p0 exp[−2 λ^4 σ_φ^2] for external Faraday dispersion (Burn law), with σ_φ^2 derived from the φ structure function at the image scale.
- Scattering from electron-density fluctuations:
  • Phase structure function: D_ϕ(r;ν) = 8π^2 r_e^2 λ^2 ∫_0^L dz ∫ d^2q [1−cos(q·r)] P_ne(q, k_∥ integrated)
  • Define diffractive scale r_diff by D_ϕ(r_diff;ν)=1; then τ_sc(ν) ≈ (D_eff/c) (λ/2π r_diff)^2 with D_eff = s(1−s)D.
  • Predict Δν_d ≈ (2π τ_sc)^{-1}.
- RM time increments:
  • Use r = v_eff Δt to map temporal increments to transverse separations through the screen.
  • Predict RM structure function D_RM(r) from the spectra of n_e and B_∥ (including cross-term) under the same anisotropic power laws.
B4. Validation on synthetic turbulence cubes (required):
- Generate 3D random fields δn_e, δB with the above cross-spectra (FFT-based spectral synthesis), include anisotropy and inner/outer scales.
- Ray-trace or phase-screen propagate to produce synthetic I(ν,t), τ_sc(ν), and polarization with external Faraday rotation/dispersion.
- Sample synthetic data on the *actual* observing cadence/gaps and channelization.
- Demonstrate parameter recovery under three data regimes:
  (i) RM-only: quantify which parameters are non-identifiable (expected: C_n^2 and l_i poorly constrained).
  (ii) RM + τ_sc: show recovery of C_n^2 and β improves and enables τ_sc prediction.
  (iii) RM + τ_sc + depolarization: show recovery of ρ_{nB} and σ_φ improves.
- Pre-register success criteria: calibrated posteriors (SBC rank statistics near uniform), and out-of-sample predictive coverage for τ_sc and depolarization.

C. Mandatory Directive (3): Identifiability of geometric vs turbulence separation
C1. Geometric component model (explicit, low-dimensional):
- RM_geo(t)= Σ_{m=1}^{M} [A_m cos(mΩ t)+B_m sin(mΩ t)] with Ω=2π/P_orb; M≤3 unless data demand.
- Alternative: orbital-phase basis using known/fit P_orb with prior from Asset 1-like periodicity.
C2. Turbulence component model (increment hierarchy, now tied to forward spectra):
- Instead of an abstract multiplicative cascade alone, we use a hybrid:
  • Large-scale statistics constrained by the spectral forward model (Section B),
  • Intermittency captured via log-Poisson modulation of local RM increments: ΔRM(r) = ΔRM_Gauss(r) × exp(I_r), where I_r is a scale-dependent intermittent field with She–Leveque parameters (to be inferred) but constrained not to alter second-order scaling implied by β.
C3. Simulation-based calibration (SBC) for geometry–turbulence separability:
- Generate ensembles under: (i) pure turbulence, (ii) turbulence+geometry, (iii) turbulence with intermittent bursts that create pseudo-periodic runs, (iv) irregular cadence with seasonal gaps.
- For each ensemble, fit the full model and compute:
  • Geometry detection power: P(select geometry | geometry true)
  • False positive rate: P(select geometry | no geometry true)
  • Bias in inferred turbulence β, anisotropy a, and intermittency parameters.
- Pre-register acceptance thresholds (example): false-positive rate <5% at matched cadence; geometry amplitude recovered within 1σ for injected S/N≥X; and turbulence slope bias <0.1.

D. Mandatory Directive (2): Minimal, falsifiable E–RM operator with nested models
D1. Intrinsic energy model (starquake-like but not overinterpreted):
- True radiated energy distribution: p(E_rad) = broken power law with parameters (α1, α2, E_b), or tapered power law; fitted hierarchically with per-instrument completeness.
D2. Separation of intrinsic vs extrinsic polarization/RM measurability:
- Define a latent intrinsic polarization coherence parameter κ_int per burst.
- Nested models:
  • H0 (screen-only): κ_int independent of E_rad; p(κ_int) is stationary (or depends only on measured width/spectrum).
  • H1 (energy-coupled intrinsic): log κ_int = c0 + c1 log(E_rad/E0) with c1≠0.
- External screen predicts κ_ext(ν,t) from σ_φ and scattering predicted by Section B.
- RM measurability probability:
  P(RM reliable | burst) = sigmoid( a0 + a1 S/N + a2 κ_int + a3 κ_ext(ν,t) )
- Observed fluence/energy model includes detection threshold and scattering broadening loss.
D3. Falsification via multi-band break shift:
- If extrinsic coherence loss dominates the apparent break, then the inferred completeness turn-over energy E_turn(ν) must scale with ν according to the predicted τ_sc(ν) and depolarization scaling (approximately a power law tied to β and inner scale).
- Pre-register held-out tests: fit using one band, predict E_turn in another; compare H0 vs H1 by Bayes factors / predictive log-score.

E. Mandatory Directive (4): Nuclear-physics deliverable reframed
E1. Replace EoS-weight inference with elastic-energy consistency bounds:
- Model available elastic energy E_el ≤ (1/2) μ u_break^2 V_crust, with μ and V_crust ranges from representative EoS families but treated as broad priors.
- Introduce radiative efficiency and beaming: E_rad = η f_b E_el, with priors on η and f_b (log-uniform or literature-informed bounds).
- Output: posterior on η f_b required to reconcile observed E_rad distribution with plausible E_el; report whether extreme efficiencies are required (tension test), not EoS selection.

F. Inference engine and computation
F1. Joint likelihood includes: RM posteriors, τ_sc(ν) measurements/limits, depolarization metrics, and burst detection process.
F2. Sampling: SMC / particle MCMC with gradient-free kernels for non-Gaussian latent fields; use amortized surrogates (emulators) trained on synthetic forward-model grids for expensive phase-screen predictions, validated against direct simulations.
F3. Model comparison: (i) geometry only, (ii) turbulence only, (iii) turbulence+geometry, each crossed with H0/H1 E–RM operator; evaluate on held-out epochs/bands.

G. Deliverables and success metrics
- Demonstrated synthetic identifiability boundaries (where RM-only fails; where adding τ_sc/depol succeeds).
- Posterior predictive agreement for RM increment PDFs, τ_sc(ν), depolarization trends, and energy distribution across bands.
- Falsifiable conclusion on whether the observed energy break is intrinsically set (H1) or propagation/completeness-driven (H0) via multi-band predictive tests.
- Conservative elastic-energy/efficiency bounds rather than EoS weights.
Feasibility:
1) Addressing the RM→scattering underdetermination (reviewer point i): We do not claim RM uniquely determines scattering. We explicitly parameterize the joint spectra/cross-spectra of n_e and B (including anisotropy and inner/outer scales) and *include τ_sc(ν) and depolarization in the likelihood*. We then demonstrate with synthetic turbulence cubes that RM-only cannot recover key scattering parameters (expected), but RM+τ_sc(+depol) can—thereby converting an identifiability risk into a tested requirement on the dataset. This directly meets the mandate to “write down and validate a concrete forward model” and to show when RM-only sampling is insufficient.

2) Preventing the E–RM operator from absorbing selection effects (reviewer point ii): The nested H0/H1 operator makes intrinsic energy→polarization dependence optional and testable. By forcing model selection on held-out multi-band data—especially the predicted frequency dependence of the apparent completeness break—we prevent a flexible latent intrinsic term from mimicking propagation-induced breaks. This is a pre-registered falsification pathway, not a post-hoc explanation.

3) Geometry–turbulence separability under sparse cadence (reviewer point iii): We elevate ‘cascade-consistency’ from an intuition to a quantified identifiability statement using SBC under the real cadence/gaps and adversarial intermittent-turbulence scenarios. The outcome will explicitly state the parameter regimes (cadence, amplitude, intermittency strength) where geometry can/cannot be reliably detected, preventing overclaiming.

4) Nuclear-physics deliverable realism (reviewer point iv): We demote EoS inference to elastic-energy consistency bounds conditioned on explicit efficiency/beaming priors. This reframing ensures outputs are not prior-dominated EoS weights; instead, the proposal yields robust constraints of the form “required η f_b is within/outside plausible ranges,” which is scientifically valuable and defensible.

5) Alignment with Assets 1 and 2: Asset 1 motivates the presence of a periodic geometric RM component coexisting with stochastic turbulence; we preserve that concept but replace non-identifiable additive SF decomposition with a validated forward model plus SBC-tested separation. Asset 2 motivates a starquake-like broken power law in energies; we retain it while making the propagation-induced break hypothesis falsifiable via band-dependent predictions tied to the same turbulence field that explains RM, τ_sc, and depolarization.
Critique: The proposal is technically ambitious and materially improved in identifiability discipline, but several key links remain under-specified or risk being non-identifiable in practice. (1) The ‘single 3D turbulence field’ is parameter-rich (C_n^2, C_B^2, ρ_{nB}, β, β_B, a, l_o, l_i, L, s, plus intermittency parameters and v_eff(t)), and the mapping from these to the joint set {RM(t), τ_sc(ν), Δν_d, depolarization} is not demonstrated to be uniquely constraining for FRB 20201124A-like datasets; in particular, L–C_n^2–l_o degeneracies in scattering, and n_e–B_∥ cross-term degeneracies in RM increments vs mean RM, are likely to survive even with τ_sc unless you impose informative priors or external constraints (e.g., screen distance, DM partition, independent velocity constraints). (2) The depolarization modeling mixes multiple mechanisms (external Faraday dispersion, bandwidth depolarization, scattering-induced PA decorrelation) but the proposal does not clearly separate what is predicted from φ(θ) statistics versus what is absorbed into κ_int/κ_ext; without a strict measurement model for PA coherence and L/I that accounts for intrinsic spectral/polarization variability, κ_int may remain a flexible absorber and weaken the H0/H1 falsification. (3) The geometric RM term is low-dimensional, but the ‘cascade-consistency’ separation hinges on correct turbulence scaling over the sampled time lags; real cadence gaps and limited dynamic range in Δt may make periodic vs intermittent discrimination fragile, and acceptance thresholds (e.g., bias <0.1 in β) are stated without tying them to required number of bursts, S/N distribution, or cadence window function. (4) The plan relies heavily on emulators for phase-screen predictions; however, emulator validity for tail statistics (intermittency, rare high-RM excursions, non-Gaussian depolarization) is not assured and could undermine SBC conclusions if the emulator smooths extremes. Overall, the mechanism is coherent, but the proposal still risks being underconstrained unless it commits to concrete external anchors and a tighter, testable measurement model for polarization/scattering observables beyond RM.

Hypothesis:
Binary neutron star (BNS) inspiral data in the Virgo–LIGO network can yield *calibrated* (not prior-dominated) probabilities for post-merger remnant outcome—long-lived NS (hypermassive/supramassive) versus prompt collapse—when (i) spin-orbit and spin-induced quadrupole information is extracted with waveform models that explicitly include the relevant PN structure, and (ii) the mapping from inspiral parameters to remnant stability is implemented as a *probabilistic generative model* that marginalizes over EOS and over *model-error hyperparameters* (universal-relation scatter, NR-threshold-fit scatter, waveform systematics, and angular-momentum loss/redistribution uncertainty).

Mechanistic rationale addressing identifiability: while BNS aligned spins are typically small and degenerate with mass ratio and tides, enforcing EOS-consistent co-variation among {Λ(m), I(m), Q(m,χ)} does not act as a hard restriction but as a *correlated prior/likelihood augmentation* that reduces the effective dimension of the intrinsic-structure sector. This increases the mutual information between inspiral data and the remnant class by turning weak spin-induced quadrupole signatures (entering at higher PN order) into a *multi-parameter consistency test* against tides and masses. Crucially, the proposal does not assume the universal relations or NR threshold mass relations are exact; instead, it introduces explicit scatter parameters and checks posterior calibration (coverage) on NR injections across EOS and thermal prescriptions. The hypothesis is therefore: inspiral-only remnant classification becomes both informative and well-calibrated in a quantifiable SNR/parameter regime, because the pipeline (a) measures a constrained combination of spin–mass–tidal structure that is better determined than any single small effect, and (b) propagates all dominant modeling uncertainties so that P(prompt|data) changes only when demanded by the data (validated via prior-to-posterior information gain and coverage tests).
Plan:
Step 0 — Define models, domains, and data products (pre-registered before analysis)
0.1 Events & injections: use public LIGO/Virgo BNS events (e.g., GW170817-class) plus a controlled injection grid spanning: chirp mass 1.0–1.4 M☉, mass ratio q∈[0.6,1], aligned spins χ1,χ2∈[−0.1,0.1] with additional stress-tests up to 0.2, and tidal deformabilities consistent with candidate EOSs. Include realistic PSDs across observing epochs; analyze both 2-detector and 3-detector configurations.
0.2 Waveform families (systematics control): analyze with at least two inspiral-capable models that include spin–spin and quadrupole-monopole (QM) effects: 
  • Primary: a PN/EOB inspiral model with explicit QM terms (e.g., an EOB family with tidal + spin-spin/QM support) using consistent PN order across comparisons.
  • Secondary (robustness): an alternative approximant with different resummation/implementation of tides/spin-spin (and, where feasible, an NR-hybrid injection truth model). 
Predefine the PN content to be included (spin-orbit up to the highest order available in the chosen model; spin-spin including QM; tidal up to NLO/NNLO as implemented).
0.3 Remnant labels for validation: for NR injections, define ground truth remnant class via simulation outcome (prompt collapse vs not), plus a standardized proxy for “long-lived” (e.g., survival beyond a threshold time) when available.

Step 1 — EOS ensemble and structure computation with explicit uncertainty
1.1 EOS bank: assemble hadronic + hybrid EOSs filtered by: Mmax≥2.0 M☉, thermodynamic stability, and causal sound speed c_s≤c (piecewise-polytrope or spectral parameterization). Maintain a *mixture prior* over EOSs (discrete bank weights or continuous hyperprior over spectral coefficients).
1.2 Precompute structure tables per EOS: TOV sequences giving R(m), Λ(m), I(m), and spin-induced quadrupole coefficient κ(m) (or equivalent parameterization used by the waveform). Provide interpolation with quantified numerical error.
1.3 Universal-relation model with hyperparameters: implement I–Love–Q / Love–Q relations as *probabilistic* constraints, not identities. Define hyperparameters σ_UR controlling relation scatter and possible bias terms b_UR (to absorb known approximation error at the relevant compactness/spin range). Calibrate (informative priors) using published residuals where applicable; allow posterior updating.

Step 2 — Likelihood acceleration with physics-coupled parameterization (relative binning + constrained transforms)
2.1 Relative binning backbone: implement relative binning for rapid likelihood evaluation seeded from matched-filter outputs (per Asset 1). Ensure it supports the chosen waveform families and the augmented parameter transform.
2.2 Parameterization: sample in (m1,m2,χ1,χ2, EOS or EOS-parameters, extrinsics). Deterministically map to (Λ1,Λ2,I1,I2,Q1,Q2) using EOS tables plus UR stochasticity: e.g., Q_i = Q_EOS(m_i,χ_i) × exp(δ_Qi), with δ_Qi ~ Normal(b_UR, σ_UR).
2.3 Replace hard “rejects” with soft generative factors:
  • Causality/Mmax: implement as prior support for EOS parameters/bank membership (hard only at EOS-parameter level), avoiding sharp boundaries in event-level intrinsic parameters.
  • Spin breakup: implement a smooth penalty/prior p(χ|m,EOS) that transitions near χ_K(m,EOS) with width w_K to avoid discontinuities.

Step 3 — Probabilistic remnant surrogate model (explicit definition + uncertainty propagation)
3.1 Remnant surrogate target: model the probability of prompt collapse given intrinsic parameters and EOS:
  p(prompt | M_tot, q, χ_eff, χ_a, EOS, θ_rem)
where θ_rem are surrogate hyperparameters.
3.2 Functional form: implement a calibrated probabilistic classifier tied to NR-inspired threshold mass structure:
  • Latent threshold: M_th = M_th,fit(q, χ_eff, EOS; a) + ε_th, with ε_th ~ Normal(0, σ_th).
  • Prompt indicator via smooth link: p(prompt)=sigmoid[(M_tot − M_th)/Δ], where Δ captures transition width due to thermal support, angular-momentum transport, and NR classification ambiguity.
3.3 Calibration/training data: train a and (σ_th,Δ) on an NR dataset spanning q, spin, and multiple EOS/thermal prescriptions (as in Asset 2’s logic, but extending to treat EOS/thermal differences as contributors to σ_th and potential EOS-dependent terms). Split into train/validation; report domain of validity explicitly (q range, χ range, mass range).
3.4 Angular-momentum/energy budget as a latent-variable model (no hard feasibility cut):
  • Introduce latent post-merger losses/redistribution parameters η = {f_J,GWpost, f_J,wind, f_J,mag} with priors from NR/EM-informed ranges.
  • Use inspiral-inferred J at merger proxy J_merg (computed from the inspiral model at a reference frequency/contact proxy) with an uncertainty term σ_J,model capturing waveform/systematic error.
  • Condition M_th (or Δ) on an effective support parameter depending on J_merg and η, but keep this as a probabilistic modulation, not a veto.
3.5 Output per event: posterior over remnant class with full marginalization:
  P(prompt|d)=∫ p(prompt|θ,EOS,θ_rem,η) p(θ,EOS,θ_rem,η|d) dθ dEOS dθ_rem dη.

Step 4 — Quantitative identifiability / information plan (mandatory)
4.1 Injection grid experiment: for each point in (SNR, q, χ_eff, EOS) grid, compute:
  • Prior-to-posterior KL divergence for χ_eff and for the remnant class probability (or the latent margin M_tot−M_th).
  • Mutual information I(data; remnant) estimated via Monte Carlo across the injection distribution.
  • Bayes factors comparing models with/without EOS–Q coupling (i.e., σ_UR→∞ as “decoupled” limit) to quantify when the data prefers the coupling.
4.2 Prior-dominance diagnostic: define a criterion such as |E[P(prompt|d)] − E[P(prompt)]| > k·SD[P(prompt)] with k preset, and require that this occurs alongside a minimum information gain threshold (e.g., KL(P||prior) exceeding a preset value). Report the SNR and parameter regimes where the criterion is met.
4.3 Sensitivity to spin magnitude: explicitly map performance as a function of injected χ_eff (including realistic small spins) to show whether gains persist at χ_eff~0.01–0.03 or only at higher spins.

Step 5 — Waveform-systematics control and robustness (mandatory)
5.1 Multi-approximant inference: run the full pipeline with at least two waveform families (Step 0.2). Treat waveform choice as a discrete nuisance parameter or perform model comparison; propagate differences into systematic uncertainty on P(prompt).
5.2 Synthetic waveform error model: introduce a hyperparameterized phase-error term δφ(f)=∑_k c_k (f/f0)^{α_k} in a controlled basis (small set of coefficients) with priors informed by known model discrepancies.
