1.1 Semi-analytic surrogate for maximum available elastic+magnetic release in a correlated crustal failure (dimensionally consistent):
  • Maximum shear stress supported: τmax ≈ εbreak μ̄, where μ̄ is a fault-region averaged shear modulus.
  • Fault volume: Vfault ≈ Afault ΔR.
  • Elastic energy available (order-unity geometric factor ξE to absorb detailed strain geometry):
      Eelastic,max ≈ ξE (τmax^2 / 2μ̄) Vfault = ξE (εbreak^2 μ̄ / 2) Afault ΔR.
  • Magnetic contribution available in the same region, limited by local B and volume (geometric factor ξB):
      Emag,max ≈ ξB (B^2/8π) Afault ΔR.
  • Total cutoff in the engine frame (local):
      Ec,local(ΔR, μ̄, B, εbreak, Afault) = min[ Eres(ΔR,B),  Eelastic,max + Emag,max ],
    where Eres is a global reservoir cap (computed from EOS-consistent crust and B) preventing unphysical repeated release.
1.2 Mapping Afault to ΔR (finite-thickness correlation constraint):
  • Parameterize Afault = π Lc^2 with correlation length Lc bounded by shell thickness and magnetic coupling:
      Lc = χL ΔR, with χL ∈ [0.3, 3] inferred (encodes whether ruptures are thickness-limited or laterally extended).
  • Then Afault ∝ ΔR^2 and Ec,local scales as:
      Ec,local ∝ (εbreak^2 μ̄ + B^2/4π) ΔR^3  (up to ξE, ξB, χL factors).
  • This yields a sharply testable scaling: Ec increases steeply with ΔR; nuisance parameters (ηrad,fbeam) cannot fully absorb ΔR because they enter multiplicatively on Eobs while ΔR controls both cutoff location and the event clustering timescales via the Hawkes kernel (Step 2).
1.3 Propagation to observed isotropic-equivalent burst energy (what FAST measures):
  • Observed isotropic-equivalent energy:
      Eiso,obs = (ηrad / fbeam) (Ec,local / (1+zG)) × ζspec × ζband,
    where ζspec, ζband are spectral/bandpass corrections computed from the fitted burst spectrum and instrumental band.
  • Commit to inference on ηrad and fbeam with bounded priors; report posterior on the combination ηrad/fbeam and show robustness bands for Ec→Eiso under prior extremes.
  • Deliverable: a publishable Ec-scaling section with explicit dimensional checks and a table of fiducial parameter values that yield ~10^38 erg at plausible ΔR,μ̄,B.

Step 2 — Derive the Hawkes kernel from finite-shell stress transfer (causality/stability explicit)
2.1 Physical picture translated to a stationary, causal kernel:
  • A failure at ti produces a stress perturbation δσ(r,t) that (a) propagates laterally at an effective speed vA (Alfvén/shear-Alfvén), (b) relaxes viscoelastically with timescale τrel, and (c) increases the hazard of another failure where δσ brings local stress closer to threshold.
  • Represent the incremental triggering rate as proportional to an integrated Green’s function of stress transfer over the shell:
      κ(t−ti) ∝ ∫ d^2r  W(r;Lc) Gσ(r, t−ti; vA, τrel),
    where W is a rupture/interaction kernel of range Lc.
2.2 Publishable closed-form surrogate kernel (what is implemented):
  • Use a causal, normalizable kernel motivated by wavefront propagation + exponential relaxation:
      κ(t) = (n/τd) exp(−t/τd) H(t)  with τd = sqrt(τA^2 + τrel^2),
    where H is the Heaviside function and τA ≡ Lc/vA is the Alfvén crossing time across the correlated patch.
  • Branching ratio n is not free-floating: tie it to stress-drop physics and finite energy budget:
      n = n0 × S(ΔR, εbreak, μ̄, B),  with n constrained to (0,1) for stationarity.
    Implement S as a monotone function increasing with available transferable stress fraction and decreasing when the inferred cumulative released energy approaches the reservoir cap.
2.3 Hawkes intensity with completeness/selection explicitly inside the simulator:
  • True burst process: λtrue(t)=λ0(t)+∑i κ(t−ti; ΔR,B,…) .
  • Observed process is thinned by time-varying detection probability pdet(t,E,ν,width) from completeness curves:
      λobs(t,E)=pdet(t,E,…) λtrue(t,E).
  • This is implemented as a marked thinning process in simulation; therefore selection effects are not “corrected after” but are part of the generative model.
2.4 Learnability from times alone (pre-registered diagnostic):
  • Identify τd and n primarily from (i) short-lag clustering and (ii) excess variance over Poisson after thinning; validate via simulation-based recovery under measured pdet(t,E).
  • Separate slow rate-state changes from self-excitation by including a baseline λ0(t) modeled as a piecewise-constant or spline latent state with a prior on smoothness; demonstrate via simulations that τd,n remain identifiable when λ0 varies.

Step 3 — Plasmoid RM/DM/depolarization mark model with degeneracy-breaking observables
3.1 Low-dimensional, energy-conditioned plasmoid parameterization (avoids unconstrained per-burst freedom):
  • For event i, draw baryon mass and magnetic flux from scaling relations with scatter:
      log mb,i = a_m + b_m log Ei + εm,   log Φi = a_Φ + b_Φ log Ei + εΦ,
    with small intrinsic scatters εm, εΦ to be inferred.
  • Magnetization σ0,i follows from energy partition:
      Ei = Erad,i + EB,i + Ekin,i,  with Erad,i=ηrad Ei and EB/Ekin determined by σ0.
3.2 RM/DM evolution model that generates unique multi-frequency polarization signatures:
  • Assume an expanding shell of thickness Δ with radius R(t)=R0+v t. Electron density scales as ne(t) ∝ mb / R(t)^2 Δ, and parallel magnetic field scales as B||(t) ∝ Φ / R(t)^2 (flux freezing; allow reconnection decay as exp(−t/τrec)).
  • Then the transient plasmoid Faraday rotation scales as:
      RMpl(t) ∝ ne(t) B||(t) Δ ∝ (mb Φ) / R(t)^4 × exp(−t/τrec),
    while DMpl(t) ∝ ne(t) Δ ∝ mb / R(t)^2.
  • Crucial degeneracy breaker: RMpl/DMpl ∝ Φ / R(t)^2 × exp(−t/τrec), so joint RM(t) and DM(t) (even upper limits on DM changes) constrain Φ separately from mb.
  • Additional degeneracy breaker: bandwidth-dependent depolarization. Predict polarized fraction L/I as a function of ν and time from differential Faraday rotation within the shell:
      depol(ν,t) = exp[−2 σRM(t)^2 λ^4],
    where σRM(t) is generated by the model from internal RM gradients across the emitting region; its time evolution depends differently on mb vs Φ than RM amplitude alone.
3.3 Instrumental polarization systematics control (explicit):
  • Reprocess polarization with measurement equation modeling (full Jones/Mueller calibration); propagate calibration uncertainties into RM posteriors.
  • Null tests: RM stability on calibrators; off-pulse leakage checks; repeatability across sub-bands; RM synthesis vs QU-fitting cross-validation.
  • Register an “analysis freeze” on calibration strategy prior to SBI to prevent implicit tuning.
3.4 External-screen alternative model (for falsification):
  • Model RMscreen(t) as an independent stochastic process (e.g., OU or DRW) with optional orbital-like deterministic term; crucially, enforce that RMscreen has no event-locked dependence on Ei.
  • Compare models using identical completeness and identical baseline-rate flexibility to avoid unfair advantage.

Step 4 — PSR B1744-24A role tightened to pipeline validation only
4.1 Use PSR B1744-24A to validate that deterministic geometric RM templates can be recovered and subtracted with correct uncertainty propagation:
  • Fit RM(t)=RM0 + g(phase; A,ϕ0, harmonics) + ε(t) and verify recovery of g and residual statistics under injected systematics.
  • Deliver a public “template subtraction + error propagation” module.
4.2 Do NOT impose PSR-derived amplitudes/periods as priors on FRB 20201124A. For FRB 20201124A, include an optional deterministic periodic component with broad priors and demonstrate it is (or is not) supported by evidence after accounting for plasmoid marks.

Step 5 — SBI implementation with mandatory validation and minimal informative summaries
5.1 Inference target and summaries (minimal but informative, pre-registered):
  • Times/energies: (i) distribution of inter-arrival times conditional on rate state, (ii) log-likelihood of a fitted Hawkes surrogate on simulated vs observed (used as a summary), (iii) energy–waiting-time coupling (E vs next-wait and prev-wait).
  • Polarization marks: (iv) joint distribution of (Ei, ΔRM at fixed lags), (v) cross-correlation C_{E,RM}(lag), (vi) time evolution of depolarization index vs ν (or σRM(t) inferred per epoch), (vii) constraints on ΔDM if measurable.
5.2 SBI algorithm and calibration:
  • Use neural posterior estimation (normalizing flow) trained on forward simulations with explicit thinning/completeness.
  • Mandatory validation: simulation-based calibration (SBC) rank tests for all core parameters (ΔR-related EOS parameter, n, τd, b_m, b_Φ); coverage checks on credible intervals; posterior predictive checks on all summaries.
  • Model-misspecification stress tests: inject (a) unmodeled frequency-dependent selection, (b) extra RM noise floors, (c) incorrect depolarization law; quantify bias on ΔR and on energy–RM coupling.
5.3 Model comparison protocol:
  • Prefer calibrated classifier-based model selection with confusion matrices under misspecification; avoid uncalibrated approximate Bayes factors.
  • Report decision robustness as a function of simulation mismatch and prior width.

Step 6 — Pre-registered identifiability and falsification plan
6.1 ΔR recoverability:
  • Generate synthetic datasets matched to FAST completeness and cadence for FRB 20220912A (energies+times) and FRB 20201124A (energies+RM+depol). Sweep ΔR across EOS library while varying ηrad/fbeam within bounds.
  • Success criterion: posterior on ΔR (or crust-core transition pressure proxy) must achieve a pre-set resolution (e.g., 68% CI width < factor 2) in ≥80% of trials; otherwise report non-identifiability and downgrade claims to constraints on Ec only.
6.2 Energy–RM coupling uniqueness:
  • Fit coupled plasmoid model and external-screen-only model on the same synthetic truth sets; demonstrate that external-screen model cannot reproduce simultaneously (i) C_{E,RM}(lag) shape, (ii) depolarization time–frequency evolution, and (iii) RM/DM co-evolution constraints.
  • Falsification criterion on real data: if C_{E,RM}(lag) is consistent with zero for all lags AND depolarization evolution shows no event-locked signatures beyond calibration uncertainties, reject the coupled mechanism.

Deliverables (explicit)
D1. A publishable Ec scaling note with EOS→(ΔR,μ̄,zG) mapping and a table of parameter priors; code to compute Ec and Eiso,obs.
D2. A methods paper-grade derivation and validation of the finite-shell Hawkes kernel including stationarity (n<1), causality, and thinning by completeness.
D3. Open-source forward simulator: Hawkes+finite-thickness cutoff+plasmoid RM/DM/depol with selection and polarization calibration error models.
D4. Pre-registered SBI validation report: SBC, coverage, PPC, and misspecification stress tests.
D5. Results paper: joint constraints on Ec and on ΔR proxy; model-selection outcome vs external-screen alternative; empirical test of event-locked RM/depolarization signatures in FRB 20201124A.
Feasibility:
Physics-to-statistics bridge is now explicit and testable. (i) The cutoff is no longer a qualitative claim: Ec,local = [ξE(εbreak^2 μ̄/2)+ξB(B^2/8π)] AfaultΔR with Afault=π(χLΔR)^2 yields Ec∝ΔR^3 (up to bounded nuisance factors). Because ΔR also enters the Hawkes kernel timescale τA= Lc/vA and thus clustering statistics, ΔR cannot be fully absorbed by ηrad/fbeam; it is constrained jointly by (cutoff location + temporal triggering).
Identifiability is pre-registered and quantified. (ii) The Hawkes kernel is specified in a stationary causal form κ(t)=(n/τd)exp(−t/τd)H(t) with τd tied to τA and τrel; stability condition n<1 is enforced, and completeness enters as thinning using measured pdet(t,E), eliminating a major confound noted by reviewers.
Degeneracy-breaking for RM marks is concrete. (iii) RM amplitude alone is degenerate, so the plan uses joint RM(t), DM(t)/limits, and time–frequency depolarization evolution; the model predicts RMpl(t)∝(mbΦ)/R^4 and DMpl(t)∝mb/R^2, so RM/DM and depolarization evolution constrain Φ vs mb and reconnection timescale τrec. Instrumental polarization systematics are addressed with explicit calibration and null tests before SBI.
PSR B1744-24A is appropriately scoped. (iv) It is used only to validate the deterministic-template subtraction and uncertainty propagation pipeline, not as an informative prior for FRB orbital physics, meeting the reviewer mandate.
SBI is safeguarded against common failure modes. (v) The proposal mandates simulation-based calibration, coverage, posterior predictive checks, and model-misspecification stress tests, and limits summaries to a minimal informative set tied directly to kernel parameters and plasmoid physics. Model comparison is performed via calibrated classifier-based selection with robustness reporting rather than uncalibrated Bayes factors.
Empirically, feasibility is supported by data scale and complementarity: FRB 20220912A provides ≥10^3 bursts to constrain Hawkes clustering and cutoff emergence under selection; FRB 20201124A provides polarization/RM variability necessary for mark constraints; together they constrain both ΔR-linked cutoff and plasmoid-driven RM signatures in a way no single summary-statistic analysis (broken power law + SF) can. The plan includes explicit failure criteria: if ΔR is not recoverable under realistic selection in recovery tests, claims are limited to Ec constraints; if event-locked RM/depolarization signatures are absent, the coupled mechanism is rejected.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong on implementation discipline (explicit forward model, selection as thinning, priors bounded, SBC/coverage, falsification criteria) and it corrects common identifiability failures in FRB population work. The major scientific risk is that the key physical link—ΔR setting a *universal* cutoff near 10^38 erg across multiple repeaters—remains under-justified because Ec depends comparably on poorly constrained quantities (B in the failure region, Afault via χL, ξE/ξB geometry factors, and ηrad/fbeam), and the proposed Hawkes-timescale coupling may not sufficiently break those degeneracies without an independently constrained vA, τrel, and λ0(t) variability. The Hawkes kernel is physically motivated but effectively a single-exponential surrogate; it is not demonstrated that a finite-thickness magneto-elastic shell uniquely yields this kernel shape or that alternative self-exciting/clustered processes with comparable flexibility (e.g., nonstationary Poisson + renewal clustering, ETAS-like power-law kernels, or SOC-inspired marked processes) cannot reproduce the same time-energy statistics after thinning. On the RM side, the plasmoid model is plausible and the inclusion of depolarization/DM as degeneracy-breakers is methodologically sound, but it hinges on the availability of sufficiently precise, time-resolved polarization calibration and meaningful DM limits on burst-to-burst timescales—often marginal in practice. Finally, the reservoir-cap term Eres is described as EOS-consistent but not specified, and repeated-release bookkeeping can inadvertently reintroduce non-identifiability (model can trade reservoir dynamics against n, λ0(t), and ηrad/fbeam).

Hypothesis: GX 13+1’s Fe XXV/XXVI wind is launched from a narrow annulus at r_launch ≈ (1–3) r_in where magnetospheric truncation and radiation pressure jointly set the effective potential and mass-loading: (i) when r_in expands (larger r_m from lower \dot{M} or larger μ), the open magnetic flux and lever arm increase, driving a faster, lower-column, more highly ionized magneto-centrifugal/radiative-MHD wind; simultaneously the reflector solid angle and relativistic broadening decrease because the optically thick disk is truncated farther out and wind scattering increases; (ii) when r_in contracts, radiation/thermal driving dominates with lower terminal speeds, larger columns, and stronger relativistic reflection from smaller radii. The refined approach overcomes standard degeneracies by making r_in the single shared latent state that simultaneously constrains (a) the dynamical velocity scale v(r) via a pre-specified wind topology calibrated to radiative-MHD simulations (limiting model flexibility), (b) the ionization structure through self-consistent density and illumination tied to \dot{M} and geometry, and (c) timing observables through pre-registered competing QPO→r_in mappings that are adjudicated using falsifiable discriminants (energy-dependent lags, harmonic content, Q/coherence). Critically, magnetic inference will rely on local, observable diagnostics (timing geometry and transfer-source calibration) rather than kpc-scale Galactic RM priors; and EoS inference will be demoted to a conditional, systematically-marginalized secondary product rather than a headline deliverable.
Plan:
A. Data set construction (state coverage + strict simultaneity)
1) Primary target (GX 13+1): assemble strictly simultaneous or bracketed (≤12 hr) observations with: Chandra/HETG (Fe K absorption line centroids/widths; Fe XXV/XXVI), XMM-Newton/RGS (soft-band absorption/emission for density/ionization constraints where usable), NuSTAR (reflection hump + Fe emission profile; high-energy continuum), NICER (broadband continuum + high-S/N timing; energy-resolved lags).
2) State labeling: reproduce a consistent hardness–intensity and color–color classification using RXTE legacy definitions (Asset 1) mapped onto NICER/NuSTAR bands via response-folded synthetic colors; define 6–10 “analysis epochs” chosen to span: strong wind detections, weak/non-detections, and jet-coexistence regimes.
3) Timing products (per epoch): compute PSDs and cross-spectra in multiple energy bands; extract candidate QPOs (centroid ν, Q, rms), harmonic structure, coherence, and phase/time lags vs energy; compute covariance spectra to isolate variable components.
4) Spectral products (per epoch): build jointly fit spectra with instrument cross-normalizations and time-filtering matched to timing intervals; retain unbinned counts for Poisson likelihood where feasible.

B. Wind forward model: fixed topology + calibrated emulator + propagated model error
B1) Adopt a concrete wind class (pre-registered): a Blandford–Payne–like magneto-centrifugal streamline family with radiative acceleration and Compton heating/cooling (“BP+rad” hybrid), implemented as follows.
  • Streamline geometry: self-similar poloidal streamlines anchored at r0 with opening angle set by a single parameter θ0; launch annulus r0 ∈ [r_launch,min, r_launch,max] with r_launch = k r_in and k ∈ [1,3].
  • Enforced invariants along each streamline (hard constraints in the generator):
    - Mass loading κ = ρ v_p / B_p (constant on a streamline)
    - Field-line angular velocity Ω_F (constant)
    - Total specific angular momentum L = r v_φ − (r B_φ)/(4π κ) (constant)
    - Bernoulli integral including radiative work term W_rad (parameterized from local flux and force multiplier)
  • Acceleration components:
    - Magneto-centrifugal: determined by Ω_F and Alfvén radius r_A = λ^{1/2} r0 (λ is magnetic lever arm)
    - Radiative: line+electron scattering as an additive acceleration a_rad = (κ_es F/c) (1+M(t,ξ)), where M is a force multiplier dependent on ionization ξ and optical depth parameter t.
  • What is inferred vs fixed:
    - Inferred (global): r_in per epoch, k, θ0, λ (or equivalently r_A/r0), κ (or base density normalization), covering factor Ω/4π, microturbulence v_turb, metallicity Z_Fe (with informative prior), and a wind clumping factor f_cl (lognormal prior).
    - Fixed/parametrically limited: streamline functional form, invariant set, and allowed parameter ranges anchored to simulation calibration (below).

B2) Emulator calibration and validation (mandatory to prevent “physics-washing”)
1) Calibration grid: build/curate a published radiative-MHD simulation grid (or a community dataset) spanning NS-LMXB-relevant regimes: L/L_Edd ∈ [0.2,1.2], μ (or B) spanning 10^8–10^10 G-equivalent truncation, and inclinations i ∈ [40°,80°]. If full NS radiative-MHD grids are sparse, use: (i) radiative-MHD disk wind grids (BH/AGN-scaled) for ionization/acceleration behavior + (ii) separate magnetospheric truncation scalings for r_in; then treat mismatch as emulator error.
2) Outputs emulated: for each epoch’s continuum, emulate mappings from (r0, λ, κ, θ0, L/L_Edd, spectral shape) → profiles of v(r), n(r), and column N_H(ξ) along sightline.
3) Emulator architecture: Gaussian-process or normalizing-flow emulator with explicit uncertainty σ_emul(x); validate with held-out simulations; require ≤10–20% predictive error in v_inf and log ξ at the relevant columns for Fe XXV/XXVI (report as a validation table).
4) Likelihood propagation: include emulator error as additive covariance in the predicted optical depth τ(E): τ_pred(E) ~ N(τ_model(E), σ_emul(E)^2), ensuring posteriors broaden when the surrogate is uncertain.

B3) Photoionization and line formation (physics-anchored)
1) Compute ion fractions using XSTAR/Cloudy tables conditioned on the fitted SED; but do not fit “free” multi-zones. Instead, ionization structure follows n(r) and F(r) from the wind generator: ξ(r)=L_ion/(n r^2).
2) Line optical depths: integrate along line of sight through the streamline bundle; include velocity shear and v_turb for line broadening; predict centroids/blueshifts, equivalent widths, and line ratios Fe XXV/Fe XXVI.
3) Include electron scattering in the wind as an energy-dependent attenuation and as a contributor to reflection dilution, with τ_es tied to wind column.

C. Inner disk / magnetosphere module (latent r_in with physical bounds)
1) Parameterization: r_in,epoch = max(R_NS, η r_m), with r_m = C (μ^4/(2GM \dot{M}^2))^{1/7}. Infer μ and C×η jointly with informative priors from NS-LMXB population ranges; allow epoch-to-epoch variation via \dot{M} (from continuum) and a stochastic term δr capturing short-timescale truncation jitter.
2) Accretion viability constraints: enforce r_in < r_co (corotation) for stable accretion; if spin is unknown, treat ν_spin as a nuisance parameter with broad prior and propagate to r_co; reject propeller solutions unless data demand (model comparison).

D. Reflection + continuum with conservative systematics (EoS demoted)
1) Reflection model: use a high-density relativistic reflection suite allowing ionization gradients (radial stratification) and variable disk density; treat emissivity profile as flexible but regularized (e.g., broken power law with priors) and include wind scattering screen (from B3).
2) Systematic model components (explicit nuisance terms):
  • Density/ionization stratification hyperparameters with wide priors
  • Calibration offsets between instruments
  • A “reflection bias” term capturing unmodeled coronal geometry (broad prior on height/compactness proxies)
3) Output policy: report r_in posteriors robust to these nuisance terms; only translate to (M,R_NS) under explicitly labeled scenarios (e.g., “optimistic systematics” vs “conservative systematics”) and never as the primary success metric.

E. Timing link: pre-registered competing mappings + discriminants
E1) Pre-register 3 QPO→r_in hypotheses (no post-hoc invention)
Model T1 (Keplerian): ν_QPO = ν_K(r_in) = (1/2π) (GM/r_in^3)^{1/2}.
Model T2 (Lense–Thirring precession): ν_QPO = ν_LT(r_in, a_*) with a_* as nuisance; requires specific lag-energy signatures and coherence trends.
Model T3 (Beat-frequency family): ν_QPO = ν_K(r_in) − ν_spin (ν_spin nuisance).

E2) Discriminants beyond frequency (mandatory)
For each detected QPO, require fits to:
  • Energy dependence of fractional rms (e.g., increasing with energy vs peaking)
  • Phase/time lags vs energy at ν_QPO (hard vs soft lags; magnitude)
  • Harmonic content (presence/absence; relative phase)
  • Coherence/Q vs spectral hardness
Define a model selection criterion using Bayes factors with an Occam penalty and require that at least two discriminants favor the selected timing model; otherwise downweight timing by inflating σ_ν (treat as weakly informative).

F. Joint inference and identifiability controls
1) Bayesian engine: HMC/NUTS on the joint likelihood: L = L_spectra(counts|model) × L_timing(PSD/cross-spectra|model) × priors.
2) Identifiability checks:
  • Simulation-based calibration: generate synthetic datasets from the forward model across the parameter prior and verify recovery of r_in and wind parameters.
  • Posterior predictive checks targeting the key mechanistic coupling: correlation between absorption blueshift and reflection broadening mediated by r_in.
3) Benchmarking: compare against (i) standard multi-zone XSTAR absorption + phenomenological reflection and (ii) reflection-only fits; quantify uncertainty shrinkage in r_launch and r_in and check for prior-dominance via sensitivity to prior widening.

G. Transfer-source calibration (local magnetic diagnostics prioritized)
1) GRO J1744-28 (Asset 2): apply the same wind+reflection framework; test whether the model naturally supports large inferred r_in ~ O(10^2 GM/c^2) and high outflow velocities without unphysical energetics; use this as a calibration point for μ–r_in scaling.
2) SAX J1808.4-3658 (Asset 3): use pulse-profile/visibility constraints to inform r_in geometry in a system with known magnetic channeling; treat these as an external validation of the r_in inference machinery (not by importing its priors into GX 13+1).

H. Deliverables (re-scoped)
Primary: posterior of r_in(t), r_launch, wind \dot{M}_wind, v_inf, Ω/4π, and ion fractions; validated discrimination among timing mappings; quantified emulator error budget.
Secondary (conditional): constraints on μ/B and (M,R_NS) only under conservative systematic scenarios; explicit statement of what assumptions are required for EoS relevance.
Feasibility:
1) Addressing QPO non-uniqueness (Critique 1): the proposal no longer treats “QPO frequency → r_in” as a single deterministic link. It pre-registers three physically standard mappings (Keplerian, Lense–Thirring, beat-frequency) and requires additional, falsifiable timing observables (energy-dependent lags, harmonics, coherence/Q trends) as discriminants. If discriminants are inconclusive, the timing term is automatically weakened (inflated uncertainty), preventing model-dependent bias from dominating r_in.

2) Making the wind surrogate constrained and testable (Critique 2): the wind is not an open-ended “multi-zone” absorber. It is a fixed-topology BP+rad streamline family with explicit invariants (κ, Ω_F, L, Bernoulli+W_rad) and a small, declared set of inferred parameters (k, θ0, λ, κ, Ω/4π, v_turb, f_cl). Flexibility is further controlled by calibrating an emulator to a published radiative-MHD simulation grid and propagating emulator error into the likelihood; this prevents overconfident or overly flexible fits from reintroducing degeneracies.

3) Demoting/removing Galactic RM-based magnetic-sign priors (Critique 3; Mandatory Directive): the Galactic counterclockwise-field prior is removed from the inference pipeline because its information content for the magnetospheric/disk-wind field at ~10–10^3 km is negligible relative to local field geometry uncertainties. Magnetic inference instead comes from local/transfer diagnostics: consistency of μ with truncation-driven r_in evolution, energetics constraints, and cross-source validation against systems with magnetic channeling (SAX J1808.4-3658) and large r_in with wind signatures (GRO J1744-28).

4) Preventing overreach on EoS/TOV (Critique 4; Mandatory Directive): EoS constraints are explicitly re-scoped as secondary and conditional. Reflection modeling includes conservative systematics (ionization/density stratification, emissivity uncertainty, wind scattering) with wide priors, and results will be reported in tiered scenarios (conservative vs optimistic) with stress tests. The primary success criterion is mechanistic closure on r_in–wind coupling and robust posteriors on r_in and wind properties, not tight (M,R_NS).

5) Why identifiability is plausible in practice: GX 13+1 provides simultaneous wind + jet regimes at high luminosity (Asset 1), offering the required dynamic range where truncation and radiation both plausibly matter. The model’s key breaking of degeneracy is observationally anchored: r_in affects (a) reflection broadening and continuum geometry, while the same r_in sets the dynamical velocity scale and column distribution in the wind; observing correlated changes in Fe absorption blueshift/strength and reflection shape across epochs provides a cross-constraint that is unavailable in spectral-only fits. Transfer-source tests (Assets 2–3) provide external validation that the same r_in machinery reproduces known large-truncation and pulse-profile behaviors, reducing the risk that GX 13+1 results are an artifact of model flexibility.
Critique:
This is an unusually rigorous and self-aware proposal that directly addresses multiple known failure modes in NS-LMXB wind/reflection/timing inference. The engineering plan is detailed, technically plausible, and appropriately constrained, with explicit controls on model flexibility (fixed topology, emulator uncertainty propagation, pre-registered timing hypotheses). Logical consistency is strong: r_in is correctly identified as a physically privileged latent variable that simultaneously governs wind launching, reflection geometry, and characteristic frequencies. The proposal’s strongest feature is its explicit treatment of identifiability and degeneracy, which is rarely handled at this level of sophistication.

Score deductions arise from two areas. First, the feasibility of emulator calibration remains partially aspirational: the availability and relevance of radiative-MHD simulation grids for NS-specific luminosities, magnetic truncation, and inclination is uncertain, and the proposed hybrid calibration (BH/AGN winds plus separate truncation scalings) risks introducing correlated systematics that may be difficult to quantify beyond the stated 10–20% error. Second, while the timing discriminants are well chosen, GX 13+1’s historically complex and sometimes ambiguous QPO phenomenology raises a nontrivial risk that the timing arm will frequently downweight itself, leaving r_in primarily constrained by spectroscopy and reflection despite the joint framework.

Evidence grounding is generally excellent, but the terminal concept chain to the Galactic disk magnetic field is effectively severed by design. While this is scientifically justified and explicitly mandated, it weakens the literal fulfillment of the stated target chain rather than misusing it. The rationale quality is high: the proposal does not merely apply existing tools but restructures the inference problem around a physically motivated latent state with falsifiable couplings.

Hypothesis:
RM/DM variability in repeating FRBs is generated by a superposition of (i) a deterministic orbital-phase geometric term produced by periodic modulation of the line-of-sight through an ordered magneto-ionic structure, and (ii) stochastic magnetized plasma fluctuations with Kolmogorov-like inertial-range scaling and intermittency. The key identifiability failure in existing structure-function approaches is not merely irregular sampling, but *activity-gated sampling*: bursts occur preferentially in windows, so a red-noise plasma process observed only during those windows can masquerade as a quasi-periodic geometric signal. We hypothesize that this aliasing is broken only if burst times are treated as part of the generative model and if the turbulence-to-observables mapping is closed with a tractable, falsifiable physics parameterization.

Mechanistic refinement (addresses reviewer directives): We will implement a Causality-Constrained Marked Point-Process Radiative Transfer framework in a *minimal identifiable form* consisting of:
(1) a pre-registered, low-degree-of-freedom orbital rate-modulation g_orb(φ) (sinusoid + first harmonic) that cannot morph into arbitrary windowing; 
(2) a self-exciting clustering component g_mag(t) constrained by a FAST-motivated energy-break prior, which is *diagnostically separable* from orbital modulation because it produces phase-incoherent clustering; and
(3) a 1D line-of-sight effective-medium turbulence closure that jointly predicts the increment statistics of (DM, RM) and the scattering observable τ_sc through an explicit n_e–B_∥ cross-correlation parameter and a compressive/Alfvénic mixture.

Why this overcomes the reviewer-identified limitations: (i) The turbulence field is no longer a high-dimensional latent 3D cascade; it is reduced to a path-integrated 1D stochastic process whose parameters map uniquely to DM/RM/τ_sc via a closed set of assumptions (mode mixture + correlation coefficient + inner/outer scales). (ii) RM cannot be tuned independently of scattering/DM because the closure ties B_∥ fluctuations to density fluctuations through a small set of physically interpretable parameters that simultaneously govern Faraday rotation and phase perturbations. (iii) Non-identifiability between arrival-time modulation and mark modulation is controlled by restricting g_orb to a fixed harmonic family with tight priors, and by explicitly testing phase coherence of marks conditional on inferred orbital phase. (iv) The nuclear-physics/I(M,R) module is either (a) quantified via sensitivity analysis to show whether it prunes parameter space at all, or (b) removed from the primary model and retained as an optional second-stage interpretation layer.

Target deliverable hypothesis test: In FRB 20201124A, the model should recover a phase-locked component in RM(t) (and possibly DM/τ_sc) that remains significant after accounting for activity gating and clustering; in FRB 20121102A, the same turbulence closure should fit mark covariances without requiring any orbital term. A joint hierarchical fit should show consistent turbulence hyperparameters (within uncertainties) while allowing different or null g_orb across sources.
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-registration of the minimal identifiable model (before full inference)
0.1 Fix the functional family for orbital modulation (mandatory):
- Define orbital phase φ(t) = 2π(t − T0)/P_orb.
- Pre-register g_orb(φ) = a1 cos(φ) + b1 sin(φ) + a2 cos(2φ) + b2 sin(2φ).
- Impose shrinkage priors: (a_k, b_k) ~ Normal(0, σ_orb^2) with σ_orb ≤ 0.5 (log-rate units), and enforce ||(a2,b2)|| ≤ 0.5||(a1,b1)|| to prevent overfitting.
- Optional geometry-informed phase prior: if independent constraints exist (e.g., optical companion periodicity), use them only as weak priors on P_orb.
0.2 Fix the clustering model family (mandatory):
- Use a Hawkes process with exponential kernel: λ_H(t) = Σ_{t_j<t} κ exp(−(t−t_j)/τ_H).
- Constrain branching ratio n_b = κ τ_H < 0.8 (stationarity) with informative prior centered on values reproducing observed waiting-time tails.
0.3 Fix the turbulence-to-observables closure (mandatory, reviewer item #1): a 1D effective medium with coupled n_e and B_∥ fluctuations.
- Model line-of-sight fluctuations as increments at an effective screen or extended medium characterized by:
  • Outer scale L0, inner scale l_i, spectral index consistent with Kolmogorov (β = 11/3 fixed initially; later relax to β ∈ [3.4, 4.0] only if identifiable).
  • Intermittency parameter μ controlling non-Gaussian increments via a lognormal multiplicative cascade in 1D (wavelet-domain truncation).
  • Mode mixture f_c ∈ [0,1] (compressive fraction) with Alfvénic fraction 1−f_c.
  • Cross-correlation ρ_nB ∈ [−1,1] linking δB_∥ to δn_e.
- Closure equations (minimal, falsifiable):
  • δn_e is generated by the 1D cascade (μ, L0, l_i).
  • δB_∥ = α_c f_c (δn_e/n0) B0 + α_A (1−f_c) ξ_A, where ξ_A is an independent cascade field with same μ but scaled amplitude; α_c, α_A are order-unity amplitude parameters with tight priors (log-normal around 1 with 0.3 dex scatter).
  • Impose Corr(δn_e, δB_∥) = ρ_nB by constructing ξ_A and the compressive term in a Gaussian-copula layer before applying intermittency (keeps computation tractable while preserving correlation control).
- Observables mapping:
  • DM_i = DM0 + DM_orb(φ_i) + ΔDM_turb(t_i) + ε_DM,i.
  • RM_i = RM0 + RM_orb(φ_i) + K [B0 ΔDM_turb(t_i) + n0 ΔB_∥,turb(t_i)] + ε_RM,i.
  • τ_sc,i predicted from the same δn_e spectrum via the phase structure function D_φ(ℓ) (thin-screen approximation first): τ_sc ∝ ν^{−4} SM^{6/5} with SM derived from the cascade amplitude, L0, l_i, and path length; include a single geometric factor G_sc with informative prior to absorb uncertain screen distance/lever arm. This forces δn_e amplitude to be consistent with scattering.

Step 1 — Data assembly and window-function reconstruction
1.1 Build burst-level catalogs for FRB 20201124A and FRB 20121102A:
- t_i: barycentered TOAs; observing frequency ν_i and bandwidth; facility ID.
- marks: RM_i±σ_RM,i, DM_i±σ_DM,i, τ_sc,i (or decorrelation bandwidth Δν_d) with uncertainties, p_lin,i, PA(λ^2) fit residual statistic.
- fluence/proxy and detection pipeline metadata where available.
1.2 Correct propagation/instrument systematics:
- remove ionospheric RM; standardize DM reference; polarization calibration flags.
- heteroscedastic likelihood for marks (facility-dependent error model).
1.3 Reconstruct selection function W(t) and threshold model:
- For each telescope k, infer detection efficiency η_k(F, t) from reported thresholds + cadence; marginalize over missing fluence with a simple parametric burst-fluence distribution.
- Define W_k(t) as exposure indicator; overall W(t)=Σ_k W_k(t) and incorporate η_k into the point-process likelihood.

Step 2 — Minimal CMPP-RT generative model (tractable)
2.1 Marked point-process likelihood:
- λ(t) = W(t) λ0 exp[g_orb(φ(t)) + g_env(t)] + W(t) λ_H(t).
- g_env(t) is *restricted* to a low-frequency spline with strong regularization (e.g., 3–5 knots over the full observing span, prior on second derivative) to prevent absorbing periodicity.
2.2 Marks conditional on events:
- Condition on t_i and latent turbulence state at t_i: p(m_i | t_i, θ).
- Orbital mark modulation (ordered medium):
  • DM_orb(φ) = d1 cos(φ)+e1 sin(φ) (first harmonic only, unless Bayes factor supports second harmonic).
  • RM_orb(φ) = r1 cos(φ)+s1 sin(φ) + r2 cos(2φ)+s2 sin(2φ) with shrinkage as above.
- Turbulent components ΔDM_turb(t_i), ΔRM_turb(t_i), τ_sc,i share the same cascade parameters (μ, L0, l_i) and closure (f_c, ρ_nB, amplitudes).
2.3 Turbulence parameterization (computational tractability, reviewer item #1):
- Use a 1D wavelet-domain lognormal cascade truncated to J scales (e.g., J=8–10), defined on the observing time axis under a frozen-flow mapping: spatial scale ℓ ↔ v_eff Δt.
- v_eff is a nuisance parameter with informative prior (bounded sub-relativistic; broad enough to encompass wind/screen motion), but *only enters through the ℓ–Δt mapping*; keep it shared across marks.
- Complexity: O(N J) per likelihood evaluation for N bursts (no 3D latent field).

Step 3 — Identifiability-first simulation program (mandatory reviewer item #3)
3.1 Build a simulator that generates synthetic catalogs with:
- Realistic multi-telescope W(t) patterns and detection thresholds.
- True P_orb, g_orb amplitude, Hawkes parameters, and turbulence parameters.
- Realistic mark uncertainties matching observed σ_RM, σ_DM, τ_sc errors.
3.2 Recovery threshold maps (pre-registered outputs):
- For a grid over (N_bursts, cadence gaps, σ_RM), compute posterior contraction and bias for:
  • P_orb (recoverable if |P̂−P|/P < 1% and period unimodality),
  • μ, L0, l_i (recoverable if posterior SD shrinks by ≥50% relative to prior and no multimodality).
- Report “minimum viable dataset” conditions separately for FRB 20201124A-like and FRB 20121102A-like regimes.
3.3 Non-identifiability diagnostics (mandatory reviewer item #3):
- Compare fits under nested models:
  A) g_orb=0,
  B) Hawkes off (κ=0),
  C) μ=0 (Gaussian increments),
  D) decouple RM from δn_e (ρ_nB free but τ_sc ignored) to show why τ_sc is needed.
- Require that true injected periodicity is recovered only when timing+marks are jointly modeled and that false periodicity is not induced by windowing.

Step 4 — Inference on real sources with staged complexity
4.1 Stage I (timing-only): infer λ(t) parameters (P_orb, g_orb coefficients, Hawkes κ, τ_H, spline g_env) using point-process likelihood only. This quantifies whether orbital modulation is needed *in rates*.
4.2 Stage II (marks-only given times): fit mark model with fixed/weakly-informed timing posterior to test whether orbital phase-locking appears in RM/DM beyond turbulence.
4.3 Stage III (fully joint): run joint Bayesian inference (particle MCMC or SMC-within-MCMC) for timing+marks with turbulence closure.
4.4 Cross-source hierarchical coupling:
- Share turbulence hyperpriors across FRB 20121102A and FRB 20201124A (μ, β if relaxed, intermittency prior scale), but allow source-specific amplitudes and geometry.
- Test whether FRB 20121102A prefers g_orb≈0 while FRB 20201124A prefers g_orb≠0.

Step 5 — EoS / I(M,R) module: quantify or drop (mandatory reviewer item #4)
5.1 Sensitivity analysis (before inclusion):
- Define wind/column mapping used in ordered module (single-parameter particle loading and B0 with path length). Compute how required luminosity L_w required to sustain B0 and n0 scales with I via Ė(I,Ω,B_p).
- Propagate realistic EoS priors on I (tens of %) to L_w uncertainty; compute whether posterior mass violating L_w≤ηĖ would be meaningfully reduced (e.g., by ≥20%).
5.2 Decision rule:
- If pruning power is weak (<20% reduction in excluded geometry volume), remove EoS block from core inference and reframe as optional interpretation.
- If strong, include as a hard/soft constraint in ordered-medium priors.

Step 6 — Validation, falsifiability, and deliverables
6.1 Posterior predictive checks:
- Waiting-time and clustering statistics; phase-folded burst rate;
- Phase-folded RM/DM and τ_sc vs phase;
- Joint distribution and cross-correlation of (RM, DM, τ_sc), ensuring τ_sc-consistency with inferred δn_e.
6.2 Falsifiable outcomes:
- If FRB 20201124A shows phase-locked RM but *no corresponding* τ_sc/DM behavior allowed by the closure, the ordered+closure model is falsified (forcing revision of mode mixture/correlation assumptions).
- If periodicity is only supported in rates but not in marks (or vice versa), this discriminates “activity gating” from “geometric column modulation.”
6.3 Physical outputs:
- For each source: posterior on P_orb (or null), ordered RM_orb amplitude, turbulence μ, L0, l_i, f_c, ρ_nB, and scattering-consistent SM; plus model comparison evidence for (binary+closure) vs (turbulence-only).
Feasibility:
Addresses critique (i): high-dimensional turbulence. We remove the infeasible 3D latent cascade and replace it with a 1D effective-medium cascade represented in a truncated wavelet basis (J≈8–10). This yields O(NJ) scaling with burst count N and avoids gridding a 3D MHD field. Frozen-flow mapping converts spatial scaling to time-lag scaling using a single v_eff parameter, keeping the latent dimension low.

Addresses critique (ii): missing closure between n_e and B_∥ and weak multi-mark constraints. We specify an explicit, minimal closure with (compressive fraction f_c, cross-correlation ρ_nB, and two amplitude parameters α_c, α_A) that simultaneously controls DM increments, RM increments, and τ_sc through the same δn_e spectrum. Including τ_sc (or Δν_d) is not optional; it is the constraint that fixes the δn_e amplitude/spectrum so RM cannot be freely tuned.

Addresses critique (iii): non-identifiability between rate modulation and mark modulation. We pre-register g_orb as sinusoid + first harmonic with shrinkage priors and restrict g_env to a heavily regularized low-frequency spline. Hawkes clustering is constrained by a branching-ratio prior (n_b<0.8). Identifiability is not asserted; it is demonstrated via simulation-based recovery thresholds under realistic W(t) and telescope thresholds, with nested-model comparisons explicitly designed to show when periodicity can and cannot be spuriously inferred.

Addresses critique (iv): weak leverage from EoS/I(M,R). We adopt an explicit decision gate: perform a sensitivity/pruning-power analysis first; only if EoS priors demonstrably remove a meaningful fraction of the geometric-plasma posterior volume do we include the nuclear-physics block in the core inference. Otherwise it is deferred to a second-stage interpretation to avoid ornamental complexity.

Empirical anchoring in provided assets: Asset 1 motivates the separability of geometric periodic components and stochastic components in RM, and our model specifically targets the reviewer-highlighted failure mode (windowed sampling) by treating burst times as generative. Asset 2 motivates a constrained clustering/self-excitation component via a stress-release picture with a characteristic break scale, which we incorporate as informative regularization of the Hawkes component rather than as an unconstrained extra degree of freedom.

Overall feasibility claim: the revised architecture deliberately reduces free parameters, fixes functional families, and requires simulation-based identifiability before full-scale application. This makes the inference computationally tractable for real FRB catalogs and makes the turbulence–RM/DM–scattering linkage explicitly falsifiable.
Critique: The central advance—embedding burst times (activity gating) into a joint timing+marks generative model and enforcing a multi-observable turbulence closure—is methodologically substantive and directly targets a real identifiability failure. Engineering-wise, the plan is detailed (pre-registered functional families, priors, staged inference, nested falsification tests, selection-function modeling) and plausibly tractable. However, several physics/mapping steps remain under-specified in ways that can reintroduce non-identifiability: (i) the frozen-flow mapping ℓ↔v_effΔt plus a 1D cascade on the observing time axis is a strong, source-dependent approximation; without an explicit prior/constraint tying v_eff (and effective path length) to τ_sc and to observed scintillation bandwidth evolution, v_eff can absorb phase-coherent structure and mimic (or erase) orbital signatures; (ii) the proposed RM mapping RM≈RM0+RM_orb+K[B0ΔDM + n0ΔB] is only conditionally valid—when fluctuations are small and path weighting is stable—and does not clearly handle the common case where RM variations come from localized Faraday screens with weak DM response; (iii) the “Gaussian-copula then intermittency” construction is computationally convenient but its physical interpretability for MHD mode mixtures is not demonstrated, and could bias higher-order statistics that are exactly what would distinguish intermittency from geometry; (iv) the selection-function reconstruction η_k(F,t) is described but not anchored to a concrete, auditable data product for each facility (pipeline completeness curves are rarely available), so mis-modeled completeness could still imprint apparent periodicity; (v) the identifiability program is strong in spirit, but the recovery criteria (e.g., 1% period accuracy) are not connected to the actual baseline/cadence and to known alias families for these sources, so the simulations risk being optimistic unless they replicate real window functions and telescope-dependent cadence structure. Overall: strong architecture with credible falsifiability hooks (especially τ_sc coupling), but key approximations (1D frozen-flow, RM/DM co-locality, completeness modeling) need tighter physical and observational anchoring to prevent the same aliasing problem from reappearing in different parameters.

Hypothesis: Small-scale, three-dimensional Kolmogorov-like plasma turbulence in the ionized medium surrounding high-energy compact objects (young neutron stars/magnetars and low-luminosity AGN-like FRB environments) imprints a predictable, physically constrained covariance between (i) the statistical component of dispersion/rotation-measure fluctuations and scattering, and (ii) the stability/shape of narrow HI absorption line profiles seen against embedded/persistent radio sources; this covariance propagates into an observable scaling between inferred electron-density fluctuation amplitude (C_n^2, outer scale L0) and radio luminosity via an energy-injection mechanism tied to the compact object’s spin-down or outflow power. We will test this by a methodological adaptation: a joint, turbulence-aware structure-function + line-profile forward model in which the standard SF analysis is structurally modified into a coupled multi-tracer likelihood that enforces (a) 3D Kolmogorov spectral scaling over inertial-range lags, (b) causality/energy-budget bounds linking turbulence driving to neutron-star/magnetar energetics (spin-down luminosity, nebular pressure) or accretion power, and (c) radiative-transfer constraints for HI absorption (non-negative optical depth, thermal broadening floor). This physics-constrained coupling will outperform separate (black-box or single-tracer) fits by breaking degeneracies between geometric variability, stochastic electron-density fluctuations, and neutral-gas kinematics, yielding tighter and physically admissible constraints on turbulence parameters and their connection to radio luminosity.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Assemble a target sample spanning (a) repeating FRBs with persistent radio counterparts localized with Arecibo+VLBI heritage datasets (e.g., FRB 121102-like systems), and (b) young radio pulsars in SNRs with measured DM and radio luminosity (e.g., PSR J0205+6449-like objects).
1.2 Compile multi-epoch, frequency-resolved polarization data where available (RM(t), DM(t), scattering timescale tau_sc(nu), scintillation bandwidth), and obtain/curate multi-epoch Arecibo HI absorption spectra toward suitable pulsars/compact-source sightlines (optical depth tau_HI(v) with stable calibration).
1.3 Standardize time-lag grids and spectral resolution; quantify systematics (bandpass stability, gain/temperature variations, baseline ripples) and propagate into per-epoch covariance matrices.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Adapted SF architecture (core modification): Replace the conventional single-observable structure function D_x(Delta t) decomposition into geometric + statistical components with a coupled multi-observable SF/PSD model:
- Model electron-density and magnetic-field fluctuations as a 3D Kolmogorov spectrum P_ne(k)=C_n^2 k^(-11/3) between outer scale L0 and inner scale li, and an analogous constrained spectrum for B_parallel fluctuations.
- Predict simultaneously: D_DM(Delta t), D_RM(Delta t), frequency-dependent tau_sc(nu) and angular broadening constraints using scattering theory consistent with the same C_n^2, L0, li.
- Include an explicit geometric term for binaries or periodic sightline modulation (as in SF geometric components) with a parametric orbit/phase model; enforce identifiability by requiring geometric terms to be coherent across DM/RM while stochastic terms follow Kolmogorov scaling.
2.2 HI absorption coupling (second modification): Embed a radiative-transfer forward model for the HI absorption line profile tau_HI(v) that is jointly conditioned on the ionized-medium turbulence parameters:
- Treat the CNM/WNM components as a mixture of thermally broadened Gaussians with non-thermal broadening that is linked (via pressure balance and turbulence coupling) to the same outer-scale driving that sets L0 in the ionized medium, but allowing a tunable neutral-ion coupling efficiency parameter epsilon_c.
- Enforce physical constraints: tau_HI(v) >= 0; kinetic temperature floor from line width; column density N_HI consistent with integrated tau_HI(v) and spin temperature priors.
- Use multi-epoch stability of tau_HI(v) (as in Arecibo TSAS non-detections) as a likelihood term that penalizes models predicting excessive small-scale density contrasts in the neutral phase.
2.3 Energy-injection/compact-object constraint (third modification): Add a physics-regularized prior/constraint connecting turbulence amplitude to high-energy source power:
- For neutron stars: require that the turbulent energy density and dissipation rate inferred from C_n^2 and L0 do not exceed a fraction f_turb of spin-down luminosity L_sd or nebular energy injection, and respect causality/pressure bounds in the surrounding medium.
- For FRB persistent sources: constrain driving by persistent radio luminosity and plausible nebular/accretion power; implement inequality constraints to prevent unphysical turbulence levels given observed L_radio.
This is implemented as a constrained Bayesian inference (e.g., Hamiltonian Monte Carlo with hard/soft constraint terms) over {C_n^2, L0, li, epsilon_c, geometric parameters, CNM component parameters}.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Synthetic injection tests: generate mock DM/RM/scattering/HI datasets from known turbulence parameters (including cases with/without geometric periodicity; with rare TSAS-like excursions) to verify parameter recovery, degeneracy breaking, and false-positive control.
3.2 Model comparison: quantitatively compare (A) uncoupled SF fits, (B) coupled SF without HI constraints, and (C) full coupled SF+HI+energy constraints using Bayes factors / information criteria and posterior predictive checks of all observables.
3.3 Physical cross-checks: verify recovered turbulence parameters produce consistent scattering measures and angular broadening (where VLBI constraints exist), and that inferred dissipation rates are compatible with local thermal balance.
3.4 Science deliverables: (i) posterior constraints on 3D Kolmogorov turbulence parameters near high-energy compact objects; (ii) empirical scaling between turbulence amplitude and radio luminosity with energy-budget interpretation; (iii) a decision framework to distinguish geometric (binary/orbital) variability from stochastic plasma turbulence using multi-tracer coherence; (iv) constraints on neutral-ion coupling (epsilon_c) using HI stability, informing ISM microphysics relevant to high-energy environments.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Structure-function decomposition into geometric and statistical components is empirically demonstrated for RM/DM variability with stochastic terms tied to electron-density and magnetic-field fluctuations and interpretable under Kolmogorov turbulence; Arecibo multi-epoch HI absorption work provides strong empirical priors on the rarity of large optical-depth variations (suppressing ubiquitous TSAS), enabling a powerful constraint on permissible small-scale density contrasts. VLBI+Arecibo localization and scattering constraints for FRB 121102-like systems provide independent checks on turbulence-driven broadening.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): High-energy astrophysical compact objects inject energy into surrounding plasmas (PWN/SNR/magnetar nebulae or accretion environments), naturally motivating turbulence-driving priors tied to spin-down or accretion power. Coupling ionized-plasma turbulence (DM/RM/scattering) to neutral-gas diagnostics (HI absorption stability/line shape) directly targets the multi-phase environment expected around these systems, while respecting conservation/causality and radiative-transfer constraints.
3. Comparative Advantage: Standard analyses treat DM/RM SFs, scattering, HI absorption, and luminosity as largely separate, leading to degeneracies (e.g., geometric periodicity vs stochastic turbulence; C_n^2 vs L0 trade-offs; neutral-structure contamination). The proposed adaptation structurally enforces that all observables share a single physically admissible turbulence parameter set and energy budget, using HI stability as an external ‘regularizer’ against overfitting small-scale structure. This should yield tighter, more interpretable turbulence constraints and a mechanistic link between turbulence amplitude and radio luminosity that can be falsified by multi-epoch posterior predictive checks.
Critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and physically disciplined proposal that integrates ionized and neutral ISM diagnostics under a single turbulence-and-energy-injection framework. The engineering plan is detailed and technically plausible, particularly the joint SF–scattering–HI forward model and constrained Bayesian inference. Logical consistency is strong: Kolmogorov turbulence provides the unifying mechanism, and the energy-budget priors are well motivated for neutron stars and FRB environments. Minor deductions arise from residual assumptions that are not fully stress-tested: (i) the strength and universality of neutral–ion turbulence coupling (epsilon_c) in extreme environments is uncertain and may be more environment-dependent than modeled; (ii) the causal link between radio luminosity and turbulence driving, while plausible, risks conflating correlated but indirect observables unless alternative injection channels are explicitly marginalized; and (iii) sample size limitations for systems with both high-quality HI absorption and dense DM/RM time series may reduce practical constraining power. These are not fatal flaws but do temper claims of universality and scalability.

Hypothesis: In BH–NS mergers that enter a transient black-hole-pulsar state, fast magnetosonic compressive pulses launched by magnetospheric deformation steepen into a monster shock only if the outgoing wave packet encounters a radially localized breakdown of force-free conditions (finite inertia/baryon loading) that creates a super-fast magnetosonic transition layer. We hypothesize that the location and strength of this transition layer—and thus the shock energetics that power the hot outflow and prompt EM counterparts—depend measurably on the neutron-star EOS through its control of (i) magnetospheric density supply and (ii) collapse/ringdown-driven boundary motion. Methodological adaptation: develop a physically constrained, multi-regime GRMHD–FFE hybrid solver that replaces standard ad-hoc FFE-to-MHD “density floors” with a conservative, characteristic-matched interface plus EOS-conditioned pair/baryon injection closure, ensuring causality and Rankine–Hugoniot consistency across the fast magnetosonic surface and enabling reliable prediction of shock formation and outflow observables.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Construct a suite of BH–NS merger initial data spanning NS EOS families (soft/medium/stiff; constrained to causal sound speed cs<=c and maximum mass constraints) and NS magnetic dipole inclinations.
1.2 For each EOS, precompute consistent NS structure (mass-radius, compactness, tidal deformability) and magnetospheric footpoint motion profiles through inspiral-to-plunge using GR (ensuring consistent metric evolution and BH spin).
1.3 Define a minimal microphysical injection model: EOS-conditioned surface baryon ablation + curvature-radiation pair supply, parameterized by compactness and surface gravity, producing an inertia map that is negligible in most of the magnetosphere but can become finite in current sheets and in the outgoing compressive wave.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Implement a hybrid GR solver with domain decomposition: inner region evolved with conservative GRMHD (shock-capturing, constrained transport), outer region evolved with GR force-free electrodynamics (FFE). Couple them with a new characteristic-matched interface at a moving radius r_int(t) chosen to track where magnetization sigma=B^2/(4pi rho h c^2) crosses a target threshold.
2.2 Methodological adaptation (core): replace common “density/pressure floors” and diffusive handoff with a Riemann-characteristic projection across the interface. Specifically, decompose the state into incoming/outgoing characteristic fields for the fast magnetosonic and Alfven modes; enforce continuity of the tangential E and B fields, enforce conservative flux matching for energy-momentum, and impose Rankine–Hugoniot jump conditions for compressive/fast-mode steepening when gradients exceed a shock sensor threshold.
2.3 Embed physics constraints directly: (i) enforce E·B=0 and E^2<B^2 in the FFE region via constrained transport plus a Lagrange-multiplier correction that minimally adjusts E to satisfy the invariant; (ii) enforce causal EOS in the GRMHD region using tabulated EOS with slope limiting to keep cs<=c; (iii) enforce global energy-angular momentum accounting by tracking Poynting, matter, and gravitational fluxes through world-tube surfaces.
2.4 Add an EOS-conditioned injection closure at the interface and in current sheets: inject minimal inertia consistent with the microphysical supply model (pair multiplicity + baryon ablation) rather than numerical floors; injection rate is constrained to keep sigma above a controlled bound except where the computed wave pressure forces sigma downward, enabling a physically motivated super-fast transition layer.
2.5 Diagnostics: compute (a) fast magnetosonic Mach number and the formation of a super-fast region; (b) shock formation radius and compression ratio; (c) hot-outflow enthalpy, baryon loading, and magnetization; (d) time-domain modulation from BH quasi-normal mode forcing (ringdown) imprinted on the compressive wave train.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Code verification: recover analytic/benchmark solutions—force-free wave propagation, relativistic MHD shocks, and magnetosonic mode speeds in curved spacetime; demonstrate interface stability and convergence with refinement.
3.2 Cross-regime validation: reproduce key qualitative features from prior literature assets: outgoing compressive waves/fast magnetosonic pulses (Asset 1), monster shock launching a hot outflow (Asset 2), and BH–NS-induced fast-mode waves steepening into monster shocks with a transient black-hole-pulsar configuration (Asset 3).
3.3 EOS inference test: generate synthetic multimessenger observables (prompt gamma/X transient energetics, FRB-like coherent precursor proxy based on Poynting spikes, and timing modulation linked to ringdown); quantify how inferred shock radius/strength correlates with tidal deformability and compactness. Use Bayesian model comparison to show that the adapted interface/injection model yields tighter EOS posteriors than standard floor-based hybrids.
3.4 Robustness: vary magnetic inclination, BH spin, and injection uncertainties; demonstrate that shock/no-shock bifurcation and hot-outflow baryon loading are controlled by physically interpretable dimensionless numbers (sigma profile slope, fast-mode steepening parameter, compactness-controlled injection), not by numerical artifacts.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Existing GRMHD/FFE studies already show fast magnetosonic compressive pulses that can steepen into shocks and launch hot outflows during collapse/merger; however, shock formation and baryon loading are notoriously sensitive to how inertia is introduced in nominally force-free regions. The proposed characteristic-matched interface and EOS-conditioned injection directly target this known failure mode while preserving conservation laws and invariants.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): High-energy astrophysical outflows straddle regimes from magnetically dominated (FFE-like) to inertia-dominated (MHD-like). A characteristic-based coupling respects the hyperbolic structure of both systems (fast/Alfven modes) and enforces physically correct transmission/reflection of compressive/fast magnetosonic waves, which is essential for predicting monster-shock onset. EOS constraints enter via compactness/tidal effects and causality-limited thermodynamics, connecting nuclear physics to shock energetics and hot-outflow baryon content.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with standard hybrid schemes that rely on numerical floors and diffusive handoffs, the adapted method (i) reduces spurious shock triggering/suppression by enforcing Rankine–Hugoniot-consistent steepening, (ii) yields physically interpretable control over baryon loading through an injection closure linked to EOS-dependent surface conditions, and (iii) improves multimessenger predictivity (shock radius, outflow magnetization, ringdown modulation) necessary for EOS inference from prompt EM counterparts to GW events.
Critique: This is a technically sophisticated and largely well-justified proposal that targets a genuine and widely acknowledged failure mode in current GRMHD–FFE hybrid simulations: unphysical shock triggering or suppression due to numerical floors. The characteristic-based interface, Rankine–Hugoniot enforcement, and EOS-conditioned injection closure demonstrate strong engineering resolution and clear awareness of the hyperbolic structure of both systems. Logical consistency is high, but not perfect: the causal chain linking neutron-star EOS to magnetospheric density supply and then to a sharply localized super-fast transition layer remains partly phenomenological. In particular, the microphysical injection model (pair creation plus baryon ablation) is parameterized rather than derived, and the degree to which EOS variations produce separable, observable signatures may be optimistic given degeneracies with magnetic inclination, BH spin, and uncertain plasma kinetics. Evidence grounding is strong and remains within the appropriate high-energy astrophysics domain, though some observables (e.g., FRB-like coherent precursors) are only loosely connected to the simulated quantities. The rationale is creative and clearly differentiated from standard hybrid approaches, but the proposal would benefit from a sharper analytical prediction that could be falsified independently of full-scale simulations.

Hypothesis: A collapsar GRB requires a transient proto-neutron-star (PNS) phase that injects and organizes large-scale poloidal magnetic flux which is then advected onto the nascent Kerr black hole; the resulting Blandford–Znajek (BZ) jet reaches the maximum jet energy only if the magnetic “hair” is anchored by a conducting disk/torus that delays the electromagnetic balding process. The core mechanism is that Tayler–Spruit dynamo (TSD) transport in the progenitor enforces predominantly toroidal fields and limits pre-collapse net poloidal flux, so the dominant contribution to BZ-relevant flux must arise from PNS magnetorotational amplification and flux opening during collapse; once the BH forms, jet power is set by the horizon-threading poloidal flux and BH spin, while the time-integrated energy is limited by flux retention vs. balding. Methodological adaptation: develop and apply a fully conservative, constraint-preserving GRMHD+neutrino framework in which (i) magnetic-flux evolution is tracked with a gauge-invariant horizon-flux diagnostic and (ii) disk anchoring currents are represented by an explicitly charge-conserving, resistive-electrodynamics closure calibrated to nuclear-EOS-dependent PNS neutrino-driven conductivity, thereby replacing the usual ideal-GRMHD “frozen-in” assumption that cannot quantify balding/retention or EOS-controlled PNS-to-BH flux inheritance.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Build a progenitor suite with MESA spanning rotation, metallicity, and angular-momentum transport prescriptions: (a) canonical Tayler–Spruit dynamo; (b) weakened/modified TSD efficiency; (c) fossil-field baseline. Output pre-collapse profiles (rho, T, Ye, Omega) and magnetic topology proxies (dominantly toroidal field amplitude with limited net poloidal flux).
1.2 Select 6–10 representative models that bracket outcomes (prompt BH vs. delayed BH via PNS). For each, define nuclear-physics priors using a set of finite-temperature EOS tables (e.g., soft/intermediate/stiff) that satisfy causality and observational NS mass constraints; include composition/opacity tables for neutrino transport.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Implement the methodological adaptation in a GRMHD code: couple (a) energy-momentum-conserving GRMHD in dynamical spacetime (or fixed Kerr after BH formation) with (b) gray two-moment neutrino radiation (M1) to capture PNS cooling, deleptonization, and neutrino-driven winds that set magnetospheric mass loading and conductivity.
2.2 Replace ideal-MHD with a resistive, charge-conserving electrodynamics module in the low-density funnel and disk corona: evolve E and B with a constrained-transport scheme plus an implicit stiff-source update for Ohm’s law J = sigma(E + v x B) in the fluid frame. Here sigma is not constant: it is parameterized by local thermodynamic state (rho, T, Ye) and calibrated from microphysical electron/positron and baryon scattering rates that depend on the chosen nuclear EOS and neutrino field. This explicitly models current closure that can anchor BH-threading flux.
2.3 Introduce a gauge-invariant horizon flux tracker and balding metric: compute Phi_BH(t) = (1/2)∫_H |B^r| dA on the apparent horizon and define a balding timescale tau_bald from dPhi_BH/dt under controlled “disk removed” and “disk present” experiments.
2.4 Enforce physical constraints in the solver: (i) divergence-free B via constrained transport; (ii) global energy and angular momentum budgets across PNS/BH+disk+outflow; (iii) causal EOS and subluminal characteristic speeds; (iv) baryon-loading constraint in the funnel (diagnose eta = E_dot/M_dot c^2) to ensure GRB-viable Lorentz factors.
2.5 Simulate collapse through: (a) PNS phase with magnetorotational amplification and flux opening; (b) BH formation; (c) post-BH accretion disk evolution for ~10–30 s physical time with adaptive mesh refinement focused on the horizon, disk, and funnel. For each run, compute BZ power P_BZ(t) from horizon fields and compare to P_j from energy flux at large radii.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Code validation: reproduce standard benchmarks (magnetized Bondi, Fishbone–Moncrief torus, BZ monopole/poloidal tests) in both ideal and resistive limits; confirm convergence of Phi_BH and P_BZ with resolution and resistivity.
3.2 Mechanism tests via controlled ablations:
- Turn off resistivity (ideal limit) to quantify bias in flux retention and balding.
- Replace EOS-dependent conductivity with constant sigma to isolate nuclear-physics leverage.
- Remove the PNS phase by forcing prompt BH collapse initial data to test the necessity of PNS-generated poloidal flux.
3.3 Observational syntheses and multi-messenger checks:
- Predict GRB prompt energetics via E_gamma,iso ~ ∫ epsilon_rad P_j dt (with baryon-loading-limited epsilon_rad), and maximum jet energy as E_j,max ~ ∫ P_BZ dt before tau_bald or disk depletion.
- Predict Type Ic-BL SN kinetic energy from PNS spin-down energy released pre-BH plus jet-cocoon energy deposition; compare to observed E_k distributions.
- Predict neutrino signal (luminosity/mean energy evolution) and, where rotation permits, gravitational-wave signatures (PNS non-axisymmetric activity) to link EOS/rotation to the presence/absence of a GRB.
3.4 Statistical inference: build an emulator of (Phi_BH, tau_bald, E_j,max, E_k) over the progenitor/EOS space and infer which combinations reproduce the joint GRB–Ic-BL population; explicitly report the required poloidal flux at BH formation and the minimum disk conductivity/current closure needed to delay balding.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: BZ jet power is controlled by BH spin and horizon-threading poloidal flux; TSD-dominated progenitors tend to generate mainly toroidal fields and suppress large-scale net poloidal flux, motivating a PNS-mediated flux-generation/inheritance channel. GRMHD simulations already demonstrate sustained jets when sufficient flux is present; what remains uncertain is the physically consistent retention vs. balding of this inherited flux, especially with realistic plasma conductivity and EOS-dependent neutrino microphysics.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Standard ideal-GRMHD assumes perfect flux freezing and cannot represent the electromagnetic balding process or current closure realistically in the funnel/corona, where resistivity and pair/neutrino physics matter. The adapted resistive, charge-conserving closure tied to EOS- and neutrino-dependent conductivity directly targets the limiting uncertainty: whether an external current source (disk/torus) can anchor BH magnetic hair long enough to reach observed GRB energies while respecting conservation laws, causality, and microphysical constraints.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to conventional collapsar simulations, this approach (i) quantitatively predicts the balding timescale and maximum jet energy from first-principles budgets rather than assuming persistent flux; (ii) links nuclear EOS to jet viability through conductivity, neutrino heating, and baryon loading; (iii) provides falsifiable multi-messenger predictions (neutrinos/GWs) that discriminate “prompt BH” from “PNS-then-BH” pathways and directly tests the proposed chain: TSD-limited progenitor flux → PNS-generated poloidal flux → BZ jet power/maximum energy → GRB emission → flux retention vs. balding → Ic-BL SN energetics.
Critique:
This is a technically ambitious and largely coherent proposal that addresses a real open problem in collapsar/GRB theory: whether sufficient horizon-threading poloidal flux can be generated and retained long enough to power observed GRB energies. The engineering plan is unusually detailed, particularly in its treatment of resistive electrodynamics, horizon-flux diagnostics, and EOS-dependent neutrino microphysics. The logical chain from Tayler–Spruit–limited progenitors to PNS-mediated flux generation and subsequent BZ jet energetics is well motivated and internally consistent.

Score deductions arise from two main issues. First, feasibility risk is high: simultaneously evolving full GRMHD, resistive electrodynamics, gray M1 neutrino transport, and long (10–30 s) post-BH accretion with adequate resolution is at the edge of current computational capability, especially for a suite of progenitors. While not impossible, the proposal does not clearly specify fallback strategies (e.g., dimensional reduction, staged simulations) if full fidelity proves intractable. Second, the physical calibration of conductivity remains somewhat underdetermined: mapping neutrino/EOS microphysics to an effective macroscopic sigma in the funnel/corona is nontrivial, and uncertainties here may dominate the balding timescale, potentially weakening the claimed EOS leverage unless carefully bracketed.

Despite these concerns, the proposal is firmly grounded in the relevant physics literature, avoids speculative mechanisms, and offers falsifiable predictions that would materially advance understanding of GRB central engines if successful.

Hypothesis: In atoll-source neutron-star LMXBs, the observable IXPE polarization degree and angle variability across accretion states and dipping intervals can be robustly decomposed into three physically distinct contributions—(i) polarized electron scattering in a hydrostatic boundary/spreading layer (BL/SL) anchored to the neutron-star surface, (ii) weakly polarized or depolarized emission from the disk and corona, and (iii) state- and phase-dependent attenuation and scattering in a *dynamical*, photoionized dip/wind absorber. We hypothesize that enforcing this regime separation, while coupling a minimal but self-consistent polarized radiative transfer solver for the BL/SL to a photoionization model for the atmosphere and an independent dynamical slab model for the dip material, resolves the key identifiability bottlenecks highlighted by reviewers. Specifically, N VII (supported by O VIII/Ne IX) acts not as a unique depth ruler but as a *consistency tracer* of the ionization parameter and column in the atmosphere and wind; when combined with energy-resolved PD/PA that are dominantly sensitive to the BL/SL scattering optical depth, latitude extent, inclination, and GR light bending, this framework enables a data-driven isolation of the compactness-sensitive polarization signatures. By integrating spin-induced oblateness, Doppler boosting, and polarization parallel transport as first-class parameters, and by explicitly marginalizing over disk/corona polarization contributions, the refined approach yields M/R constraints that are likelihood-driven rather than prior-dominated, while remaining computationally feasible and empirically testable with current IXPE and grating data.
Plan:
Step 1: Regime-separated source and data selection.
1. Select one benchmark atoll source with existing or proposed deep IXPE exposure (>500 ks) and confirmed dipping behavior (e.g., GX 13+1–like systems), coordinated with XMM-Newton RGS or Chandra HETGS and NICER.
2. Segment data into three regimes: (a) non-dip banana state, (b) non-dip island state, and (c) dip intervals. Only regime (a,b) are assumed to have a hydrostatic NS atmosphere/BL; regime (c) explicitly relaxes hydrostatic balance for the absorber.
3. Extract IXPE energy-resolved Stokes (I,Q,U) spectra (2–8 keV) per regime; extract grating spectra focusing on N VII Lyα/edge and corroborating O VIII/Ne IX lines; derive hardness–intensity and timing diagnostics to label state.

Step 2: Explicit emission decomposition with state-dependent priors.
1. Implement a three-component emission model:
   (i) Boundary/spreading layer (BL/SL): thermal–Comptonized emission tied to the NS surface; primary source of polarization via electron scattering.
   (ii) Accretion disk: multi-temperature disk emission with low intrinsic polarization (<1–2%), angle fixed to disk plane.
   (iii) Corona: Comptonized component with weak/moderate polarization, broad angular distribution.
2. Assign state-dependent priors informed by timing/spectral studies (e.g., increased BL fraction in banana state; stronger corona in island state).
3. Predict component-wise PD/PA signatures and variability; fit their normalizations jointly with polarization data rather than assuming a single effective emitter.

Step 3: Minimal physics core for BL/SL polarized transfer.
1. Solve polarized radiative transfer in the BL/SL using a plane-parallel or shallow-curvature slab with hydrostatic equilibrium enforced only locally.
2. Use a Kompaneets/Fokker–Planck approximation for Comptonization below ~10 keV, coupled to angle-dependent Thomson scattering matrices for Q,U; neglect V.
3. Free physical parameters: compactness u=GM/(Rc^2), inclination, BL/SL latitude extent, electron-scattering optical depth tau_es, spin frequency, and oblateness.

Step 4: Photoionization modeling with clear scope limits.
1. NS atmosphere: compute ionization balance (including N VII, O VIII, Ne IX) using XSTAR/CLOUDY microphysics on fixed T(z), n_e(z) profiles consistent with BL illumination; N VII used as a consistency check on xi and column, not as a unique depth probe.
2. Dip/wind absorber: independent photoionized slab with its own xi, column, velocity dispersion, and partial covering; include radiative acceleration and allow outflow velocities inferred from line shifts/broadening.
3. No hydrostatic constraint is applied to the dip absorber; its role is to modulate flux and polarization via absorption and scattering only.

Step 5: GR, spin, and polarization transport as first-class elements.
1. Perform GR ray tracing from the BL/SL to the observer using Schwarzschild plus Hartle–Thorne corrections for rotation-induced oblateness.
2. Include Doppler boosting and aberration from spin; parallel transport polarization vectors along geodesics.
